In line with our agent control roadmap , we are hardening our sandboxed environments by isolating and sealing them before high-risk training or evaluations begin. We’re committed to sharing these agent security best practices with our partners to improve security across the ecosystem.

We built Gemini 4 Argon with frontier-level capabilities on coding, knowledge work, cybersecurity defense, and creative writing to be a partner for developers, professionals, and enterprises while they tackle the most difficult problems. We’re grateful for the initial cohort of cyber defenders and trusted testers whose real-world evaluations and feedback will help us strengthen our systems before we release to developers, enterprises, and consumers, starting with paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers.
After the introductory period expires, the price of $4 per 1M input tokens and $20 per 1M output tokens will apply.

Koray is one of the world's foremost experts in artificial intelligence. As the SVP of Google DeepMind, he leads the development of Google DeepMind’s state-of-the art generative AI models and their integration into Google’s products at scale. Prior to his current role, he was VP of Research at Google DeepMind, where he founded the deep learning team and his team pioneered major research breakthroughs such as DQN (Deep Q-Network) and WaveNet.

relevantPassages.text: Today, we’re announcing our new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, which is rolling out to a set of trusted cyber defenders through our Fairwind Program .
Built to sustain deep reasoning across complex, long-horizon workflows, Argon is fundamentally changing the way we work and build at Google.
It delivers frontier performance to help in complex workflows across real-world software engineering, enterprise knowledge work like legal and finance, and cybersecurity defense.
Argon can autonomously find, validate, and patch critical software vulnerabilities.
For trusted defenders and our own internal teams at Google, we’ll be releasing Argon without cyber guardrails so they can leverage its full frontier-level cybersecurity defense capabilities.
When the model has the headroom to think deeply and generate hundreds of thousands of tokens in a single trajectory, it adds a new level of depth in reasoning to solve tough problems in one go.
It’s helping teams build faster and push the boundaries of engineering productivity and accelerating breakthroughs:

Defending against prompt injection attacks: Argon is also our most resilient model yet against indirect prompt injections, where malicious instructions or context are used to hijack a model’s behavior.
These are complex attacks that require constant vigilance and multiple layers of defense.
Google engineers have been using Argon for their daily tasks, from everyday debugging to large-scale codebase migrations and algorithm designs.

On CWE-bench v1 , which evaluates the model’s ability to remediate security vulnerabilities, Argon ties for first place with a top score of 68%, building on 3.8 Flash Cyber’s frontier performance on CWE-bench v0 .
Safely releasing frontier capabilities at this level requires a phased approach.
We are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model access while we gradually expand access.
We’ll continue to gather feedback from early testers as we iterate on guardrails before making Argon available to developers, enterprises, and consumers as soon as possible.
Argon will launch at an introductory price 1 of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price.
Beyond coding, Argon is the leading model on the Vals Index , which measures economic impact across finance, coding, legal, and tax work, with every sector weighted by its contribution to U.S.

We see similarly leading performance across other domain specific evaluations, like Vals Finance Agent v2 (multi-step financial research) and Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark (legal research and drafting).

In an early demonstration of its impact, the model uncovered a critical vulnerability exposing sensitive personal information across healthcare software used by hospitals worldwide, identifying a severe risk that previous frontier models had missed.
These safeguards underwent robustness testing by internal and external red teams using a combination of manual and automated attack methods.
It’s able to drive professional chart analysis, identify details from long videos, and take action based on a series of documents.

We used a similar system to monitor our training runs and send alerts to a dedicated incident response team, taking careful precautions against feeding the findings back into training so as to not risk shaping Argon’s reasoning to evade our monitoring.

We strongly encourage the rest of the industry to preserve reasoning transparency in these pivotal moments of increased capabilities while navigating alignment risks, so that model thoughts remain helpful in identifying and diagnosing misalignment.

Monitoring for misalignment: In order to prevent Argon from stepping out of bounds to try to accomplish a task in a way that goes beyond the user’s intentions, we are deploying misalignment mitigations that monitor Argon’s chain-of-thought and actions and stop execution when necessary.

sources.title: Google announces Gemini 4 Carbon, its latest frontier AI model that you can't use
passages: It’s almost like Google’s got something to prove after taking a break from releasing new frontier AI models earlier this year.
Just two weeks after rolling out Gemini 4 Argon , Google has announced Gemini 4 Carbon .
This isn’t the Flash model equivalent we’ve been waiting for but, rather, is an improvement on Argon, and like that model, Google is working on a staged release that could take a while.
Google says the model shows a “significant leap” in vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation.
Carbon is also apparently twice as likely to generate code that is free of vulnerabilities versus Argon.
Meanwhile, the Chrome team claims that Carbon is 10 times better at generating “high-quality” patches compared to non-Google models.
Google also notes that Carbon has increased its score by 89 points on WebDev Arena , now ranking at number four on the leaderboard.
In the Grey Swan evaluation, Carbon resisted every attempted prompt-injection attack.
That 0 percent score is better than Argon (0.7 percent), Opus 5.5 (1 percent), and GPT-6 Astra (8.5 percent).
Google has some numbers to support these vague assessments (below), showing Carbon at the top of the charts.
Google positions Carbon as a totally new model, but for all we know, it could be a post-training upgrade of Argon.
The two models have a lot in common, but Carbon does best Argon by slim margins in every test Google has given it.
Benchmarks don’t tell the whole story, of course, and it’s notable that every frontier model scores in the same neighborhood in these tests.
The gap between Carbon and the competition is just a few points.
Carbon will probably arrive first for AI Ultra subscribers and developers using the Gemini API.
Like Argon, Google will temporarily offer a discounted API rate of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.
That price will double once the introductory period expires.
Argon’s discounted rates are only good through the end of November, but Google doesn’t specify a date for Carbon.
Google has declined to provide an end date when asked, suggesting it hasn’t decided when the price will increase.
Stop me if you’ve heard this one before: Google says its latest AI model reaches a new threshold in coding, agentic tasks, and scientific analysis.
It’s so capable, in fact, that Google can’t let you use it just yet.

The post points to cybersecurity and long-horizon tasks, meaning complicated jobs that take many steps or run for a long time, as Carbon’s biggest strengths. Credit: Screenshot: Artificial Analysis SEE ALSO: Google says Gemini 4 Argon agents beat 'Minecraft' without human help The pace at which AI companies are releasing new frontier models has accelerated sharply in recent months, as the frontier AI labs race to have the best model available. 22, OpenAI shipped GPT-6 Astra earlier that month, and Google announced Argon on Sept. 30 before releasing it to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers on Oct. Each lab has claimed a new lead within weeks of the last.As with Argon, Google is announcing Carbon well before most people can use it. Carbon is starting with a small group of cybersecurity defenders, and Google hasn’t said when it will reach everyone else. (Last week's PHP2Shell incident shows just how much havoc new AI models could wreak on the internet at large.) Announcing early lets Google claim the top spot on the leaderboards now. It also gives everyone a look at the benchmarks before the next round of releases.Gemini 4 Carbon: BenchmarksIn Google’s comparison table, Carbon posts the top score on 15 of 17 benchmarks against Argon, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Fable 5.1. All figures in this section are as reported by Google. Credit: Google The two benchmarks Carbon doesn’t win are worth noting. Claude Opus 5.5 leads on OSWorld-2.1, which measures how well a model can operate a computer.A big change from Argon is that Google now reports Terminal-Bench 4.0 scores run by Artificial Analysis, an independent testing firm, rather than its own. For quick context, Terminal-Bench 4.0 measures how well an AI model can complete real technical tasks — like installing software or fixing broken code — by typing commands into a computer’s terminal on its own. It's one of the hardest agentic tests for LLMs.This is notable because the scores companies reported for each other’s models didn’t always line up with independent testing. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, Carbon jumps about eight points over Argon and moves ahead of Opus 5.5.Google also says Carbon can work on difficult engineering problems for days at a time. Artificial Analysis runs a range of tests itself and combines them into a single composite score.On the newly updated version 5.0, Carbon (high) scores 59, one point ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (max). Gemini 4 Carbon's score of 59 is leaps above Argon's 50. Credit: Artificial Analysis The scores can’t be directly compared to the previous version of the index, where Argon (High) scored 53. A one-point lead is also thin enough that the next release from OpenAI or Anthropic could easily erase it. Carbon and Meta’s Muse Wonder Full are both flagged on the leaderboard as having no publicly available API, so they can’t yet be used outside their companies’ own access programs.Gemini 4 Carbon: Safety and safeguardsGoogle says Carbon uses the same safety system as Argon, which includes monitoring the model’s reasoning, and adds more work on alignment, or keeping the model behaving as intended. According to Google’s own testing, Carbon is also better behaved than its predecessor. Google says Carbon never successfully cheated on Terminal-Bench 4.0, meaning it never found a shortcut that passed a task without actually doing the work, and it tried to cheat only 0.4 percent of the time. During internal coding work, high-severity misalignment alerts, which flag a model acting in ways its developers didn’t intend, dropped by nearly 80 percent. Carbon also makes about half as many unsupported claims as Argon. And on Gray Swan’s prompt injection benchmark, which tests whether hidden instructions can hijack a model, Carbon blocked every attack attempt, improving on Argon’s 0.7 percent attack success rate.All of these figures come from Google’s own testing.How to try Gemini 4 CarbonFor now, you can’t use Gemini 4 Carbon unless you’re an approved cyber defender in Google’s Fairwind Program. Starting this week, Carbon is rolling out to a small group of those testers, and Google says it will gradually add more trusted partners. Developers, businesses, and consumers will get access after that, but Google hasn’t given an exact public launch date.If we use Argon to figure out a timeline, about two weeks passed between its announcement and its arrival in the Gemini app for Pro and Ultra subscribers. Though we won't be able to confirm whether Google will commit to that same schedule for Carbon.When Carbon does reach the API, Google says it will cost the same as Argon’s introductory price:$2 per million input tokens$10 per million output tokensCached input tokens at 95 percent off the input priceThat keeps Carbon well below its main rivals.

Though we won't be able to confirm whether Google will commit to that same schedule for Carbon.When Carbon does reach the API, Google says it will cost the same as Argon’s introductory price:$2 per million input tokens$10 per million output tokensCached input tokens at 95 percent off the input priceThat keeps Carbon well below its main rivals.

Carbon is starting with a small group of cybersecurity defenders, and Google hasn’t said when it will reach everyone else. (Last week's PHP2Shell incident shows just how much havoc new AI models could wreak on the internet at large.) Announcing early lets Google claim the top spot on the leaderboards now.

28, Koray Kavukcuoglu, SVP at Google DeepMind, the company’s frontier AI lab, called Carbon Google’s strongest model yet. (Kavukcuoglu is leading Google DeepMind now that former CEO Demis Hassabis has stepped aside.) The post points to cybersecurity and long-horizon tasks, meaning complicated jobs that take many steps or run for a long time, as Carbon’s biggest strengths.
Each lab has claimed a new lead within weeks of the last.As with Argon, Google is announcing Carbon well before most people can use it.
22, OpenAI shipped GPT-6 Astra earlier that month, and Google announced Argon on Sept.

Artificial Analysis runs a range of tests itself and combines them into a single composite score.On the newly updated version 5.0, Carbon (high) scores 59, one point ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (max).
All figures in this section are as reported by Google.
Carbon also makes about half as many unsupported claims as Argon.

The script repeats, with one more step toward caution.

Google also reports a 26% drop in cases where the model does more than asked (overreach) and 29% in those where it does less (under-service).

The defenses remain the layered ones already seen with Argon, spanning training and real-time checks, plus monitoring of the internal reasoning.

A model that, with guardrails off, finds 88% of the vulnerabilities in a public benchmark and exploits more than half of them shouldn't go to just anyone, and both Google and Anthropic are right about that.
What remains is the question of the yardstick.
As long as leaderboards reward models the public can't use, the number 59 is a promise.
An authoritative promise, measured by a third party, but a promise without a date all the same.

The next day Google presents a model with a name and a price list, as well as a score, that few can touch.
These are two different strategies for the same tension, telling the world how capable the machines are at offense while keeping them away from anyone who might misuse them.
The Google DeepMind post on X sums up the positioning in two lines.

Use is limited to authorized activities such as threat simulations and reverse engineering, along with defensive malware analysis, phishing-resistant authentication and tracked access, and reselling access is prohibited.
Applications go through a form and Google replies to eligible candidates without giving a timeline.
A government agency or a security company in any of those markets can apply to Fairwind.
The program page doesn't list excluded countries, but Google checks the security track record and conduct of applicants before replying.
It means the model was tested without the filters that normally make it refuse dangerous requests, such as writing attack code.
It's the right way to measure raw capability and explains why Google keeps access restricted.
Whoever uses it in production will work with protections on and with usage monitoring, and the real numbers from their work could differ.

Starting this week only a subset of cyber defenders can use it, and for developers, businesses and consumers alike Google says "as soon as possible," with no date attached.
Google also says Carbon falls under the US government's voluntary process for pre-release testing.
The Google employee quoted back then said Carbon "feels like Opus 5.5," and today Artificial Analysis puts it at 59 against Opus 5.5's 58.
The comparison, though, was about coding, while the index also measures agents and general knowledge, along with scientific reasoning.
Google lists the first two as a new state of the art and notes they were measured "without guardrails," meaning without the protections active in production.
Google presents Carbon as "our next frontier model," arriving just two weeks after Gemini 4 Argon .
Argon was announced on September 30 for Fairwind participants only and opened to the public on October 13 , in the Gemini app for Pro and Ultra subscribers and in the paid API.
The script repeats, with one more step toward caution.
On WebDev Arena, the user-voted leaderboard for building websites and applications, Google reports a jump of 89 Elo points that puts Carbon in fourth place with 1768.
On the general index the comparison holds, while on coding alone the published numbers don't allow a verdict.
There's no app, no paid plan and no API key you can request.
To use a Google model that's available today, the route is Argon, described in the guide on Argon in Antigravity with the separate quota .
Three third-party judgments, all relayed by Google, round out the picture.
The Chrome team says Carbon generates high-quality patches more than 10 times better than another major frontier model, without naming which one.
Wiz , a cloud security company, sees it leading on web penetration testing benchmarks.
These are claims read in Google's post, not accounts published by the two companies.
The Argon safety report helps explain why the doors stay ajar.

Google writes there that it can't rule out that the model without protections has reached the "Cyber Uplift Level 1" threshold, the one at which an attacker would receive significant help for high-impact operations, and that it built a safety case with additional measures for that reason.
If Carbon does better than Argon on cyber, as Google states, the logic of a gradual rollout weighs even more.
Google supplies the name and the price, along with the ranking, but puts a gate in front of the door.
Like Anthropic with its Cyber Verification Program , Mountain View entrusts a list of vetted defenders with the phase in which the model can do the most damage.
Neither lab has had its figures independently replicated, and a direct comparison of frontier models on cyber remains, for now, an exercise in reading press releases.
Artificial Analysis is an independent firm that pits AI models against a battery of tests and ranks them in a single leaderboard.
The Fairwind Program, a name that will keep coming up, is the channel through which Google hands cyber defense tools to governments, critical infrastructure operators and vetted security companies.
Both are needed to read the announcement, which at first glance looks like one more launch with a record-setting ranking and on a second look is mostly about a decision on access.
In the live coding environments used internally, high-severity misalignment alerts reportedly fell by almost 80%.
Compared with Argon, claims not backed by evidence have roughly halved.
Google also reports a 26% drop in cases where the model does more than asked (overreach) and 29% in those where it does less (under-service).
On the Gray Swan IPI Benchmark, a test of prompt injection, meaning the hidden commands in the texts the agent reads, the rate of successful attacks goes from Argon's 0.7% to 0.0%.
The defenses remain the layered ones already seen with Argon, spanning training and real-time checks, plus monitoring of the internal reasoning.

A model that, with guardrails off, finds 88% of the vulnerabilities in a public benchmark and exploits more than half of them shouldn't go to just anyone, and both Google and Anthropic are right about that.
What remains is the question of the yardstick.
As long as leaderboards reward models the public can't use, the number 59 is a promise.
An authoritative promise, measured by a third party, but a promise without a date all the same.
On October 27 Anthropic published the research in which one of its unreleased models builds working exploits for Chrome, Safari, Windows, Linux and Android , already patched by the vendors.
The next day Google presents a model with a name and a price list, as well as a score, that few can touch.
These are two different strategies for the same tension, telling the world how capable the machines are at offense while keeping them away from anyone who might misuse them.
The Google DeepMind post on X sums up the positioning in two lines.

Use is limited to authorized activities such as threat simulations and reverse engineering, along with defensive malware analysis, phishing-resistant authentication and tracked access, and reselling access is prohibited.
Applications go through a form and Google replies to eligible candidates without giving a timeline.
A government agency or a security company in any of those markets can apply to Fairwind.
The program page doesn't list excluded countries, but Google checks the security track record and conduct of applicants before replying.
It means the model was tested without the filters that normally make it refuse dangerous requests, such as writing attack code.
It's the right way to measure raw capability and explains why Google keeps access restricted.
Whoever uses it in production will work with protections on and with usage monitoring, and the real numbers from their work could differ.
For an overview of Google's foundation models, their family and the differences between versions, there's the guide to foundation models with Google's models .

coreStoryFacts.text: Today, we’re announcing our new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, which is rolling out to a set of trusted cyber defenders through our Fairwind Program .
Built to sustain deep reasoning across complex, long-horizon workflows, Argon is fundamentally changing the way we work and build at Google.
It delivers frontier performance to help in complex workflows across real-world software engineering, enterprise knowledge work like legal and finance, and cybersecurity defense.
Argon can autonomously find, validate, and patch critical software vulnerabilities.
For trusted defenders and our own internal teams at Google, we’ll be releasing Argon without cyber guardrails so they can leverage its full frontier-level cybersecurity defense capabilities.
When the model has the headroom to think deeply and generate hundreds of thousands of tokens in a single trajectory, it adds a new level of depth in reasoning to solve tough problems in one go.
It’s helping teams build faster and push the boundaries of engineering productivity and accelerating breakthroughs:

Defending against prompt injection attacks: Argon is also our most resilient model yet against indirect prompt injections, where malicious instructions or context are used to hijack a model’s behavior.
These are complex attacks that require constant vigilance and multiple layers of defense.
Google engineers have been using Argon for their daily tasks, from everyday debugging to large-scale codebase migrations and algorithm designs.

On CWE-bench v1 , which evaluates the model’s ability to remediate security vulnerabilities, Argon ties for first place with a top score of 68%, building on 3.8 Flash Cyber’s frontier performance on CWE-bench v0 .
Safely releasing frontier capabilities at this level requires a phased approach.
We are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model access while we gradually expand access.
We’ll continue to gather feedback from early testers as we iterate on guardrails before making Argon available to developers, enterprises, and consumers as soon as possible.
Argon will launch at an introductory price 1 of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price.
Beyond coding, Argon is the leading model on the Vals Index , which measures economic impact across finance, coding, legal, and tax work, with every sector weighted by its contribution to U.S.

We see similarly leading performance across other domain specific evaluations, like Vals Finance Agent v2 (multi-step financial research) and Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark (legal research and drafting).

In an early demonstration of its impact, the model uncovered a critical vulnerability exposing sensitive personal information across healthcare software used by hospitals worldwide, identifying a severe risk that previous frontier models had missed.
These safeguards underwent robustness testing by internal and external red teams using a combination of manual and automated attack methods.
It’s able to drive professional chart analysis, identify details from long videos, and take action based on a series of documents.

We used a similar system to monitor our training runs and send alerts to a dedicated incident response team, taking careful precautions against feeding the findings back into training so as to not risk shaping Argon’s reasoning to evade our monitoring.

We strongly encourage the rest of the industry to preserve reasoning transparency in these pivotal moments of increased capabilities while navigating alignment risks, so that model thoughts remain helpful in identifying and diagnosing misalignment.

Monitoring for misalignment: In order to prevent Argon from stepping out of bounds to try to accomplish a task in a way that goes beyond the user’s intentions, we are deploying misalignment mitigations that monitor Argon’s chain-of-thought and actions and stop execution when necessary.
It’s almost like Google’s got something to prove after taking a break from releasing new frontier AI models earlier this year.

sources.title: Google announces Gemini 4 Carbon, its latest frontier AI model that you can't use
passages: It’s almost like Google’s got something to prove after taking a break from releasing new frontier AI models earlier this year.
Just two weeks after rolling out Gemini 4 Argon , Google has announced Gemini 4 Carbon .
This isn’t the Flash model equivalent we’ve been waiting for but, rather, is an improvement on Argon, and like that model, Google is working on a staged release that could take a while.
Google says the model shows a “significant leap” in vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation.
Carbon is also apparently twice as likely to generate code that is free of vulnerabilities versus Argon.
Meanwhile, the Chrome team claims that Carbon is 10 times better at generating “high-quality” patches compared to non-Google models.
Google also notes that Carbon has increased its score by 89 points on WebDev Arena , now ranking at number four on the leaderboard.
In the Grey Swan evaluation, Carbon resisted every attempted prompt-injection attack.
That 0 percent score is better than Argon (0.7 percent), Opus 5.5 (1 percent), and GPT-6 Astra (8.5 percent).
Google has some numbers to support these vague assessments (below), showing Carbon at the top of the charts.
Google positions Carbon as a totally new model, but for all we know, it could be a post-training upgrade of Argon.
The two models have a lot in common, but Carbon does best Argon by slim margins in every test Google has given it.
Benchmarks don’t tell the whole story, of course, and it’s notable that every frontier model scores in the same neighborhood in these tests.
The gap between Carbon and the competition is just a few points.
Carbon will probably arrive first for AI Ultra subscribers and developers using the Gemini API.
Like Argon, Google will temporarily offer a discounted API rate of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.
That price will double once the introductory period expires.
Argon’s discounted rates are only good through the end of November, but Google doesn’t specify a date for Carbon.
Google has declined to provide an end date when asked, suggesting it hasn’t decided when the price will increase.
Stop me if you’ve heard this one before: Google says its latest AI model reaches a new threshold in coding, agentic tasks, and scientific analysis.
It’s so capable, in fact, that Google can’t let you use it just yet.

sources.title: Google launches Gemini 4 Carbon, but only cyber defenders can use it - Pasquale Pillitteri
passages: Gemini 4 Carbon (which many people search for as Gemini Carbon) is Google's new flagship model, unveiled on October 28, 2026 by Koray Kavukcuoglu, the executive who leads the company's AI architecture.
It ranks first on the Artificial Analysis v5 index with 59 points, but access stays closed.
Starting this week only a subset of cyber defenders can use it, and for developers, businesses and consumers alike Google says "as soon as possible," with no date attached.
Google also says Carbon falls under the US government's voluntary process for pre-release testing.
The Google employee quoted back then said Carbon "feels like Opus 5.5," and today Artificial Analysis puts it at 59 against Opus 5.5's 58.
The comparison, though, was about coding, while the index also measures agents and general knowledge, along with scientific reasoning.
Google lists the first two as a new state of the art and notes they were measured "without guardrails," meaning without the protections active in production.
Google presents Carbon as "our next frontier model," arriving just two weeks after Gemini 4 Argon .
Argon was announced on September 30 for Fairwind participants only and opened to the public on October 13 , in the Gemini app for Pro and Ultra subscribers and in the paid API.
The script repeats, with one more step toward caution.
On WebDev Arena, the user-voted leaderboard for building websites and applications, Google reports a jump of 89 Elo points that puts Carbon in fourth place with 1768.
On the general index the comparison holds, while on coding alone the published numbers don't allow a verdict.
There's no app, no paid plan and no API key you can request.
To use a Google model that's available today, the route is Argon, described in the guide on Argon in Antigravity with the separate quota .
Three third-party judgments, all relayed by Google, round out the picture.
The Chrome team says Carbon generates high-quality patches more than 10 times better than another major frontier model, without naming which one.
Wiz , a cloud security company, sees it leading on web penetration testing benchmarks.
These are claims read in Google's post, not accounts published by the two companies.
The Argon safety report helps explain why the doors stay ajar.

Google writes there that it can't rule out that the model without protections has reached the "Cyber Uplift Level 1" threshold, the one at which an attacker would receive significant help for high-impact operations, and that it built a safety case with additional measures for that reason.
If Carbon does better than Argon on cyber, as Google states, the logic of a gradual rollout weighs even more.
Google supplies the name and the price, along with the ranking, but puts a gate in front of the door.
Like Anthropic with its Cyber Verification Program , Mountain View entrusts a list of vetted defenders with the phase in which the model can do the most damage.
Neither lab has had its figures independently replicated, and a direct comparison of frontier models on cyber remains, for now, an exercise in reading press releases.
Artificial Analysis is an independent firm that pits AI models against a battery of tests and ranks them in a single leaderboard.
The Fairwind Program, a name that will keep coming up, is the channel through which Google hands cyber defense tools to governments, critical infrastructure operators and vetted security companies.
Both are needed to read the announcement, which at first glance looks like one more launch with a record-setting ranking and on a second look is mostly about a decision on access.
In the live coding environments used internally, high-severity misalignment alerts reportedly fell by almost 80%.
Compared with Argon, claims not backed by evidence have roughly halved.
Google also reports a 26% drop in cases where the model does more than asked (overreach) and 29% in those where it does less (under-service).
On the Gray Swan IPI Benchmark, a test of prompt injection, meaning the hidden commands in the texts the agent reads, the rate of successful attacks goes from Argon's 0.7% to 0.0%.
The defenses remain the layered ones already seen with Argon, spanning training and real-time checks, plus monitoring of the internal reasoning.

A model that, with guardrails off, finds 88% of the vulnerabilities in a public benchmark and exploits more than half of them shouldn't go to just anyone, and both Google and Anthropic are right about that.
What remains is the question of the yardstick.
As long as leaderboards reward models the public can't use, the number 59 is a promise.
An authoritative promise, measured by a third party, but a promise without a date all the same.
On October 27 Anthropic published the research in which one of its unreleased models builds working exploits for Chrome, Safari, Windows, Linux and Android , already patched by the vendors.
The next day Google presents a model with a name and a price list, as well as a score, that few can touch.
These are two different strategies for the same tension, telling the world how capable the machines are at offense while keeping them away from anyone who might misuse them.
The Google DeepMind post on X sums up the positioning in two lines.

Use is limited to authorized activities such as threat simulations and reverse engineering, along with defensive malware analysis, phishing-resistant authentication and tracked access, and reselling access is prohibited.
Applications go through a form and Google replies to eligible candidates without giving a timeline.
A government agency or a security company in any of those markets can apply to Fairwind.
The program page doesn't list excluded countries, but Google checks the security track record and conduct of applicants before replying.
It means the model was tested without the filters that normally make it refuse dangerous requests, such as writing attack code.
It's the right way to measure raw capability and explains why Google keeps access restricted.
Whoever uses it in production will work with protections on and with usage monitoring, and the real numbers from their work could differ.
For an overview of Google's foundation models, their family and the differences between versions, there's the guide to foundation models with Google's models .

Google presents Carbon as "our next frontier model," arriving just two weeks after Gemini 4 Argon . Argon was announced on September 30 for Fairwind participants only and opened to the public on October 13 , in the Gemini app for Pro and Ultra subscribers and in the paid API. The script repeats, with one more step toward caution. This time there is no date for the public.

On capabilities, Google claims progress in coding and agentic tasks (the ones where the model works on its own across multiple steps), then in scientific research, full-stack web development, and understanding of images, video and audio. The Google DeepMind post on X sums up the positioning in two lines. State of the art in cybersecurity and in long-horizon tasks.
Gemini 4 Carbon is our next frontier model. It's state-of-the-art across cybersecurity and long-horizon capabilities.

Gemini 4 Carbon is first on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 with 59 points, but the margin is a single point over Claude Opus 5.5, which appears on the same page with 58 in the "Max" configuration and 57 in the "Xhigh" one. Carbon's score refers to the "High" mode.

The new version of the index, v5, aggregates nine evaluations (including Terminal-Bench 4.0, FrontierCode 2.0 and HLE-Diamond) across four categories that each carry 25% of the weight, namely agents, coding, general capabilities and scientific reasoning. The page doesn't explain what changed from v4, and that detail matters, because a reshuffled index moves the rankings even without new models (we noted this when Artificial Analysis declared the gap with open source closed ).

On WebDev Arena, the user-voted leaderboard for building websites and applications, Google reports a jump of 89 Elo points that puts Carbon in fourth place with 1768. So the lead on Artificial Analysis doesn't repeat everywhere, and among the comments on the announcement on r/singularity some readers made the same point from the other side, a model at the top of the leaderboard that almost nobody can try yet. As for the October 10 leak , when a Google employee compared it to Opus 5.5 at writing code, the numbers vindicate it only in part. On the general index the comparison holds, while on coding alone the published numbers don't allow a verdict.

In cybersecurity tests Gemini 4 Carbon reaches 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro (finding vulnerabilities), 54.8% on ExploitGym (actually exploiting flaws) and 71.0% on CWE-bench (fixing vulnerable code). Google lists the first two as a new state of the art and notes they were measured "without guardrails," meaning without the protections active in production.

Three third-party judgments, all relayed by Google, round out the picture. The Chrome team says Carbon generates high-quality patches more than 10 times better than another major frontier model, without naming which one. Wiz , a cloud security company, sees it leading on web penetration testing benchmarks. These are claims read in Google's post, not accounts published by the two companies.

The least flashy part of the post is the one describing the model's behavior. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, a test in which the agent works in a terminal and can look for improper shortcuts, Google says it brought successful cheating down to 0.0% (attempts to 0.4%). In the live coding environments used internally, high-severity misalignment alerts reportedly fell by almost 80%.

Compared with Argon, claims not backed by evidence have roughly halved. Google also reports a 26% drop in cases where the model does more than asked (overreach) and 29% in those where it does less (under-service). On the Gray Swan IPI Benchmark, a test of prompt injection, meaning the hidden commands in the texts the agent reads, the rate of successful attacks goes from Argon's 0.7% to 0.0%. The defenses remain the layered ones already seen with Argon, spanning training and real-time checks, plus monitoring of the internal reasoning.

The Argon safety report helps explain why the doors stay ajar. Google writes there that it can't rule out that the model without protections has reached the "Cyber Uplift Level 1" threshold, the one at which an attacker would receive significant help for high-impact operations, and that it built a safety case with additional measures for that reason. If Carbon does better than Argon on cyber, as Google states, the logic of a gradual rollout weighs even more.

Today Gemini 4 Carbon is available to a subset of cyber defenders chosen by Google, effective the week of the announcement. Other trusted partners will follow through the Fairwind Program , while for developers, businesses and consumers the commitment is generic. Google also says Carbon falls under the US government's voluntary process for pre-release testing.

The Fairwind program counts more than 650 partners worldwide and prioritizes governments, national cybersecurity authorities, critical infrastructure operators (healthcare, telecommunications, energy, financial networks), large platforms and academic labs. Those who join accept precise rules. Use is limited to authorized activities such as threat simulations and reverse engineering, along with defensive malware analysis, phishing-resistant authentication and tracked access, and reselling access is prohibited. Applications go through a form and Google replies to eligible candidates without giving a timeline.

The introductory price matches Argon's, $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens discounted by 95%. Once the introductory period ends, which the post doesn't date, rates rise to $4 and $20. A price list that very few people can actually pay today.

In the United States, the United Kingdom and the rest of the world there is nothing to activate. There is no app and no open API to subscribe to, and Google hasn't named countries or dates. A government agency or a security company in any of those markets can apply to Fairwind. The program page doesn't list excluded countries, but Google checks the security track record and conduct of applicants before replying.

On October 27 Anthropic published the research in which one of its unreleased models builds working exploits for Chrome, Safari, Windows, Linux and Android , already patched by the vendors. The next day Google presents a model with a name and a price list, as well as a score, that few can touch. These are two different strategies for the same tension, telling the world how capable the machines are at offense while keeping them away from anyone who might misuse them.

Anthropic shows a result with no name and no date. Google supplies the name and the price, along with the ranking, but puts a gate in front of the door. Like Anthropic with its Cyber Verification Program , Mountain View entrusts a list of vetted defenders with the phase in which the model can do the most damage. Neither lab has had its figures independently replicated, and a direct comparison of frontier models on cyber remains, for now, an exercise in reading press releases.

My view is that the gate is the right call and that this isn't enough to make the rest credible. A model that, with guardrails off, finds 88% of the vulnerabilities in a public benchmark and exploits more than half of them shouldn't go to just anyone, and both Google and Anthropic are right about that. What remains is the question of the yardstick. As long as leaderboards reward models the public can't use, the number 59 is a promise. An authoritative promise, measured by a third party, but a promise without a date all the same.

Short answer. No, unless you're part of the group of cyber defenders Google selected this week. There's no app, no paid plan and no API key you can request. Opening it up to developers, businesses and consumers is announced as "as soon as possible," with no date. To use a Google model that's available today, the route is Argon, described in the guide on Argon in Antigravity with the separate quota .

Answer. Google doesn't say. Argon remains the Gemini 4 model open to the public, while Carbon is presented as the next frontier model, with a phased access path. In the safety report Argon is described as the first model in the Gemini 4 series, so other models in the family were already in the plans.

Answer. It means the model was tested without the filters that normally make it refuse dangerous requests, such as writing attack code. It's the right way to measure raw capability and explains why Google keeps access restricted. Whoever uses it in production will work with protections on and with usage monitoring, and the real numbers from their work could differ.

The comparison, though, was about coding, while the index also measures agents and general knowledge, along with scientific reasoning. The original leak is covered in the article on the internal Gemini 4 Carbon checkpoint .

extraction.body: Maybe it's the one that’s compatible with your phone, as an Apple or Android user. Or maybe it's Amazon's Alexa, if you already own one of the many speakers that the company launched following the 2014 arrival of the first Amazon Echo. Amazon's smart-speaker fleet, in particular, is expansive, often seeing multiple new models every year, while the offerings are much narrower for Google and Apple. That said, a few months ago, Google did launch a new smart speaker for the first time in years—the 2026 Google Home Speaker—and I share my thoughts on it in this guide. After trying nearly every single smart speaker that's come out in the last decade, I have a sense of the best options available today to fit various needs. Also, check out my guides to the Best Alexa Speakers, Best Google Speakers, and Best Smart Displays if you want more insight into each category. Updated September 2026: I've added details about Amazon’s increased prices and which speakers were affected, and noted that the Google Nest Hub Max is currently out of stock online. Google's latest smart speaker, the Google Home Speaker (8/10, WIRED Recommends), is an amalgamation of great features from other smart speakers. It shares its name with the original Google speaker from 2016, but its shape and size are reminiscent of an Apple HomePod Mini. It has the tap controls and fun colors I remember from the older Google Nest Mini. And it joins the rest of Google’s smart speakers (other than the Google Pixel Tablet with the charging dock) by using Google Gemini as the default assistant instead of Google Assistant. Gemini does sound impressively human, offering answers that approximate an interaction with another person. But Google Gemini is nonetheless a touch smarter than other assistants in its cohort; it’s able to answer questions about my own schedule and knows to check with me about my artist preference if a song I request has multiple covers. Gemini for Home is free, but some features you might like to use are hidden behind paywalls. For instance, Google rebranded its video camera subscriptions to “Google Home Premium,” which bundles some smart-home assistant features and video storage into one price. There are two tiers: Standard ($10 per month or $100 per year), which includes 30 days of event-based video history, intelligent alerts for things like familiar faces and packages, Gemini Live, and an AI-based tool to help you create smart-home routines for your household. Gemini Live is the main behind-the-paywall feature you might want; it lets you switch your smart speaker into a more conversational mode. Using this feature, I had a long, natural-feeling chat with my speaker that covered my 3-year-old’s sleep patterns, scalp sunburns, and the previous night’s Love Island episode. Gemini Live doesn't work on every Google speaker, but in addition to working on the Google Home Speaker, it also works on all three versions of its available smart displays, including two iterations of the Nest Hub. My favorite is the 10-inch Nest Hub Max; it doubles as a digital photo frame powered by Google Photos, which works much better than Amazon's clunky uploader and might even be a tool you're already using. Google accounts get up to 15 GB of free storage (that'll include any Gmail or Drive files, too), so there are a lot of photos you can store and display on this device. The 10-inch touchscreen is a great size for everything from controlling your smart home and streaming videos to pulling up recipes and enjoying your own photos. Many of these capabilities rely on the smart display, which means you couldn't access them with a screen-free smart speaker. It's not the only smart display option on the market, but it has a prettier interface than Amazon's Echo Show 11 (below), and unlike on the Show 11, you won't see any ads sliding onto the screen on this Nest. There's also a camera for video calls and gesture-based controls. While there’s no cover for the camera, you can disable it if you prefer. Most of the smart speakers I spot in friends' homes come from the Amazon Echo line. Such dated speakers are still fairly well-supported, though not all of them can gain access to Alexa+, Amazon's newer AI-powered voice assistant. But even if your smart speaker can use Alexa+, it's only worth the upgrade if you have Amazon Prime, which includes access to the assistant. Without a Prime subscription, you'd have to pay $20 a month for Alexa+ on its own. It's literally cheaper to get Amazon Prime ($15 a month for most plans), which comes with a wider range of benefits. This price model is surely intentional, as it may serve as a push to get you to sign up for Prime if you haven't already. The Echo Dot Max is one of Amazon's newest models. It launched in late 2025, taking the small form from past Dot models and upgrading the device with impressive sound quality, a built-in smart-home hub, Alexa and Alexa+ access, and a slightly different look. I tested it against the latest Echo Studio last year and found the speakers were more similar in quality than I expected. The Dot Max is more expensive than older Dot models; if you don’t need next-level sound, the more affordable Echo Dot (fifth gen) might be a good fit for your needs.

sources.title: Amazon turns its most capable smart speaker into a smart camera, too
passages: Beyond audio capabilities, Amazon sees people using the speaker as a smart camera, allowing them to remotely check on a room in the home to see, for example, “how the dog is doing or make sure you didn’t leave the lights on.”
Since debuting in 2019, Amazon’s Echo Studio targeted users who wanted superior audio quality from their Alexa-based smart speaker.
The latest Echo Studio adds another less-expected differentiator: an integrated camera.
The Echo Studio with Home Camera, released alongside a pile of other Alexa devices today, doesn’t have many audio upgrades over the standard Echo Studio.
Each speaker has one 3.75-inch high-excursion woofer and three full-range drivers.
They both support Dolby Atmos and Amazon’s proprietary algorithm for adding a surround sound-like effect to stereo audio.
Per the devices’ product pages, the speakers have lossless HD audio, Advanced Room Adaptation, and features for fighting noise distortion.
Amazon announced the Advanced Room Adaptaion today, saying that the feature “continuously tunes the sound to your space, automatically adapting to the room’s acoustics.”

Amazon has a notable past when it comes to smart cameras, including previously giving cops access to data from Ring smart cameras without user consent and allegations from the Federal Trade Commission that its employees illegally spied on Ring users (Amazon eventually settled the FTC’s lawsuit for $5.8 million without admitting any wrongdoing).
These incidents may lead some privacy-focused customers to opt for camera-less alternatives.
Both speakers have four-microphone arrays and the same AZ3 Pro processor that Amazon introduced a year ago .

Pull out a board game box and ask Alexa+ to explain the rules or hold up a cereal box and Alexa can recognize it and help you reorder more flavors.

The Echo Dot is getting an overhaul and is now available for purchase in four colors alongside the upgraded Amazon Echo Studio with Home Camera . The major news here today on the Echo speaker side of things is the all-new Amazon Echo Studio with Home Camera – it adds “adds visual intelligence to Amazon’s best-sounding speaker” that allows Alexa to “see and help.” The Home Camera edition is largely the same as the previously-released model otherwise, delivering the same “powerful audio architecture” that makes for Amazon’s best sounding speaker by way of the high-excursion woofer, full-range drivers, Dolby Atmos, and Advanced Room Adaptation – “continuously tunes the sound to your space, automatically adapting to the room’s acoustics.” It also sports Adaptive Volume – “adjusts to where you are so your music or audiobook maintains the same volume as you move about.” However, it also now carries a built-in camera allowing Alexa to gain visual intelligence. This enables Live View in the Alexa app so you can “check in on the room when you’re away,” but Alexa can also “see and understand” what it’s looking at too: Pull out a board game box and ask Alexa+ to explain the rules or hold up a cereal box and Alexa can recognize it and help you reorder more flavors. Soon, you will also be able to pair the Echo Studio with Home Camera with a compatible Fire TV device to bring video calls to the big screen, making it easy to catch up with family and friends from the comfort of your living room. It very much looks the same, save for the new colorways, but Amazon says the new Amazon Echo Dot is the most capable yet. A sort of catch-all, anywhere type of home speaker, the spherical design is back, alongside the 3D knit finish, it sounds like the real upgrades here come by way of the built-in smart home hub for the first time, Amazon’s custom-designed AZ3 silicon, and the internal sound reproduction system: And we’ve made it even better. A full-range driver built into the housing creates more back volume for crisp vocals and 50% more bass than the last generation. And with Omnisense, our custom sensor fusion platform, Echo Dot can sense the environment around it, detecting things like room temperature and presence so Alexa can make your home more responsive—turning up the thermostat when the room is too cold, or turning on the lights as you walk in.” FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. extraction.body: Maybe it's the one that’s compatible with your phone, as an Apple or Android user. Or maybe it's Amazon's Alexa, if you already own one of the many speakers that the company launched following the 2014 arrival of the first Amazon Echo. Amazon's smart-speaker fleet, in particular, is expansive, often seeing multiple new models every year, while the offerings are much narrower for Google and Apple. That said, a few months ago, Google did launch a new smart speaker for the first time in years—the 2026 Google Home Speaker—and I share my thoughts on it in this guide. After trying nearly every single smart speaker that's come out in the last decade, I have a sense of the best options available today to fit various needs. Also, check out my guides to the Best Alexa Speakers, Best Google Speakers, and Best Smart Displays if you want more insight into each category. Updated September 2026: I've added details about Amazon’s increased prices and which speakers were affected, and noted that the Google Nest Hub Max is currently out of stock online. Google's latest smart speaker, the Google Home Speaker (8/10, WIRED Recommends), is an amalgamation of great features from other smart speakers. It shares its name with the original Google speaker from 2016, but its shape and size are reminiscent of an Apple HomePod Mini. It has the tap controls and fun colors I remember from the older Google Nest Mini. And it joins the rest of Google’s smart speakers (other than the Google Pixel Tablet with the charging dock) by using Google Gemini as the default assistant instead of Google Assistant. Gemini does sound impressively human, offering answers that approximate an interaction with another person. But Google Gemini is nonetheless a touch smarter than other assistants in its cohort; it’s able to answer questions about my own schedule and knows to check with me about my artist preference if a song I request has multiple covers. Gemini for Home is free, but some features you might like to use are hidden behind paywalls. For instance, Google rebranded its video camera subscriptions to “Google Home Premium,” which bundles some smart-home assistant features and video storage into one price. There are two tiers: Standard ($10 per month or $100 per year), which includes 30 days of event-based video history, intelligent alerts for things like familiar faces and packages, Gemini Live, and an AI-based tool to help you create smart-home routines for your household. Gemini Live is the main behind-the-paywall feature you might want; it lets you switch your smart speaker into a more conversational mode. Using this feature, I had a long, natural-feeling chat with my speaker that covered my 3-year-old’s sleep patterns, scalp sunburns, and the previous night’s Love Island episode. Gemini Live doesn't work on every Google speaker, but in addition to working on the Google Home Speaker, it also works on all three versions of its available smart displays, including two iterations of the Nest Hub. My favorite is the 10-inch Nest Hub Max; it doubles as a digital photo frame powered by Google Photos, which works much better than Amazon's clunky uploader and might even be a tool you're already using. Google accounts get up to 15 GB of free storage (that'll include any Gmail or Drive files, too), so there are a lot of photos you can store and display on this device. The 10-inch touchscreen is a great size for everything from controlling your smart home and streaming videos to pulling up recipes and enjoying your own photos. Many of these capabilities rely on the smart display, which means you couldn't access them with a screen-free smart speaker. It's not the only smart display option on the market, but it has a prettier interface than Amazon's Echo Show 11 (below), and unlike on the Show 11, you won't see any ads sliding onto the screen on this Nest. There's also a camera for video calls and gesture-based controls. While there’s no cover for the camera, you can disable it if you prefer. Most of the smart speakers I spot in friends' homes come from the Amazon Echo line. Such dated speakers are still fairly well-supported, though not all of them can gain access to Alexa+, Amazon's newer AI-powered voice assistant. But even if your smart speaker can use Alexa+, it's only worth the upgrade if you have Amazon Prime, which includes access to the assistant. Without a Prime subscription, you'd have to pay $20 a month for Alexa+ on its own. It's literally cheaper to get Amazon Prime ($15 a month for most plans), which comes with a wider range of benefits. This price model is surely intentional, as it may serve as a push to get you to sign up for Prime if you haven't already. The Echo Dot Max is one of Amazon's newest models. It launched in late 2025, taking the small form from past Dot models and upgrading the device with impressive sound quality, a built-in smart-home hub, Alexa and Alexa+ access, and a slightly different look. I tested it against the latest Echo Studio last year and found the speakers were more similar in quality than I expected. The Dot Max is more expensive than older Dot models; if you don’t need next-level sound, the more affordable Echo Dot (fifth gen) might be a good fit for your needs.

Pull out a board game box and ask Alexa+ to explain the rules or hold up a cereal box and Alexa can recognize it and help you reorder more flavors.

extraction.body: Alongside the reveal of the all-new Echo Show 16 at $100 off , Echo Time smart alarm clocks, and Alexa Photo Frame , Amazon has also unveiled the next-generation Echo smart speakers. The Echo Dot is getting an overhaul and is now available for purchase in four colors alongside the upgraded Amazon Echo Studio with Home Camera . The major news here today on the Echo speaker side of things is the all-new Amazon Echo Studio with Home Camera – it adds “adds visual intelligence to Amazon’s best-sounding speaker” that allows Alexa to “see and help.” The Home Camera edition is largely the same as the previously-released model otherwise, delivering the same “powerful audio architecture” that makes for Amazon’s best sounding speaker by way of the high-excursion woofer, full-range drivers, Dolby Atmos, and Advanced Room Adaptation – “continuously tunes the sound to your space, automatically adapting to the room’s acoustics.” It also sports Adaptive Volume – “adjusts to where you are so your music or audiobook maintains the same volume as you move about.” However, it also now carries a built-in camera allowing Alexa to gain visual intelligence. This enables Live View in the Alexa app so you can “check in on the room when you’re away,” but Alexa can also “see and understand” what it’s looking at too: Pull out a board game box and ask Alexa+ to explain the rules or hold up a cereal box and Alexa can recognize it and help you reorder more flavors. Soon, you will also be able to pair the Echo Studio with Home Camera with a compatible Fire TV device to bring video calls to the big screen, making it easy to catch up with family and friends from the comfort of your living room. It very much looks the same, save for the new colorways, but Amazon says the new Amazon Echo Dot is the most capable yet. A sort of catch-all, anywhere type of home speaker, the spherical design is back, alongside the 3D knit finish, it sounds like the real upgrades here come by way of the built-in smart home hub for the first time, Amazon’s custom-designed AZ3 silicon, and the internal sound reproduction system: And we’ve made it even better. A full-range driver built into the housing creates more back volume for crisp vocals and 50% more bass than the last generation. The AZ3 chip enables “advanced on-device processing for faster, more natural conversations with Alexa+.” There’s also the addition of a fourth mic so Alexa can hear you better “as you move around the room” alongside Voice ID so it knows who is talking: “Voice ID can recognize who’s speaking and personalize your experience, like playing your favorite playlist instead of your partner’s. And with Omnisense, our custom sensor fusion platform, Echo Dot can sense the environment around it, detecting things like room temperature and presence so Alexa can make your home more responsive—turning up the thermostat when the room is too cold, or turning on the lights as you walk in.” FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More. Justin is a senior deal Jedi over at 9to5Toys where he heads up our game/app coverage and more. He also covers all things music for 9to5Mac, including the weekly Logic Pros series exploring music production on Mac and iOS devices

Beneficiaries who receive Social Security before May 1997, or who receive both Social Security and SSI, are paid on the 3rd of the month.

If you count on Social Security to cover rent, groceries, or medications, you probably already have your payment dates memorized. But this November, the calendar throws a small wrench into the usual rhythm for one group of beneficiaries.

It's not a sign of a policy change or a cut to your senior benefits . It's simply the way the calendar lines up this year. Here's what's different, who it affects, and when the rest of November's payments are expected to land.

Social Security retirement, survivor, and disability checks go out on a predictable payment schedule tied to your birth date, according to the Social Security Administration (SSA). But Supplemental Security Income (SSI), a separate program for people who are blind, have a qualifying disability, or are 65 and older with limited income and resources, is typically paid on the first of the month.

When the first of the month falls on a weekend or federal holiday, the SSA moves that SSI payment to the last business day before it. Because those shifts don't happen every month, the schedule can look different from one month to the next, even though nothing about your benefit amount has changed.
Shopping for cheaper auto insurance? Enter your zip code here to get started.

November 1, 2026, falls on a Sunday. Under SSA's standard rule, when a payment date lands on a weekend, the payment moves earlier to the preceding business day. That means SSI recipients should expect their November payment on Friday, October 30, 2026, rather than on the first of the month as usual.

This isn't a delay. It's actually the opposite. The payment arrives a couple of days early precisely because the SSA doesn't let scheduled payments fall on a weekend. Still, if you're used to seeing that deposit on the first, seeing it a few days earlier in your account can be disorienting if you're not expecting it.

Beneficiaries who receive Social Security before May 1997, or who receive both Social Security and SSI, are paid on the 3rd of the month. For November 2026, that payment is scheduled for Tuesday, November 3, according to SSA's published payment calendar.
Retirement and survivor benefits for others follow the standard birth-date payment schedule with one exception:

Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) follows the same birth-date schedule as retirement benefits, according to the SSA. There's no separate calendar for disability payments. If you receive SSDI and were born between the 1st and 10th, for example, you'd expect your November payment on November 10, just like a retired worker born in that same window.

To recap, SSI recipients should expect their November payment on Friday, October 30, 2026, instead of the first of the month, because November 1 falls on a Sunday. If you also receive Social Security alongside SSI, remember your Social Security portion follows the 3rd-of-the-month rule explained above, while your SSI portion shifts to October 30.

Context helps explain why even a short delay can matter. The estimated average monthly Social Security retirement benefit for January 2026 is $2,071, according to the SSA's 2026 cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) fact sheet, reflecting a 2.8% COLA that took effect that January.
For comparison, the average disabled worker receives $1,636.47 per month as of September 2026, and the maximum federal SSI payment for an eligible individual is $994 per month in 2026, per the SSA.

It's also worth checking your earnings record periodically through your mySocialSecurity account. Since benefits are calculated from your highest 35 years of earnings, an error in your record could quietly shrink your future payment. A financial advisor can also help you weigh claiming strategies against your broader retirement picture.

November's payment schedule isn't a sign that anything has gone wrong with Social Security. It's a routine calendar adjustment that happens whenever the first of the month lands on a weekend, something that occurs several times a year without any change to benefit amounts or program rules. But it's important to know, especially if you're living on just Social Security .

Beyond this month's shift, it's worth bookmarking SSA's official payment calendar so you always know which Wednesday applies to your birth date, and so a holiday or weekend shift never catches you off guard. sources.title: Apple announces all-new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, its first touchscreen Mac - 9to5Mac
passages: Apple has officially announced the all-new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, its first touchscreen laptop.
While Apple has innovated with multi-touch on the iPhone and iPad, the Mac has been resistant to touch input for years.
Back in March, Apple upgraded the standard 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pro laptops to the current M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.
MacBook Pro features Touch for the first time, bringing pros a whole new way to interact with their content.
Crafted specifically for the Mac, every touch interaction feels incredibly responsive and refined.

Everyday tasks are simple and intuitive, allowing users to scroll through a webpage with a natural swipe; pinch to zoom in on a photo; drag and drop slides from one presentation to another; and double-tap a window to fill the screen, or flick to tile it into place.
And the touch sensor is built directly into the display panel — not layered on top of it — reducing latency so users feel like they’re touching the content itself.
Apple also touts the use of a new hinge technology in the MacBook Pro, in part to support touch input without compromising on stability:
The existing MacBook Pro configurations from March stick around at the same prices.
You just lose OLED, the glowing Apple logo, and the thinner and lighter design.
The new machines still use Touch ID with no Face ID support.
We’ll have to keep waiting for Face ID and built-in cellular connectivity.
Pre-orders are available starting today with deliveries starting November 6.
The new machine was first hinted at by Apple on October 19 with the company’s “Pro and tell” experience teaser .
Earlier today, new Apple CEO John Ternus shared a “spotlight” teaser for the laptop as well.
Remember when Apple introduced the Touch Bar?
It was supposed to be a big deal, but eventually Apple removed it.
Now they’re adding a touchscreen to the MacBook.
Apple’s Mac lineup consists of MacBook, MacBoo…
The new MacBook Pros look awesome with glowing Apple logos.
Touch also introduces entirely new ways of working for pro users.

In addition, a newly designed hinge provides greater stability while using Touch, and advanced video stabilization automatically smooths the camera feed in real time while using Touch on a video call.
Playing piano on the touchscreen MacBook Pro pic.twitter.com/lDlwIeqErd
I can’t help wondering whether Steve Jobs would have approved of this direction.
Check out 9to5Mac on YouTube for more Apple news:
The Dynamic Island now comes to Mac, serving as the home for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI.

The new machine was first hinted at by Apple on October 19 with the company’s “Pro and tell” experience teaser . Earlier today, new Apple CEO John Ternus shared a “spotlight” teaser for the laptop as well.
Read on for all the details about the new high-end laptop…
The new machine features a light-up Apple logo, tandem OLED, and touch input on the display.
It runs on the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, like the existing MacBook Pro models without OLED touch displays.
John Ternus, who is rocking a new profile picture with the new Mac, shared the first look at the new machine on X:
We’re glowing with excitement over the new MacBook Pro. You’ve gotta touch it to believe it. pic.twitter.com/BLiGkGaefL
Apple previously used a glowing Apple logo on its notebook hardware for years until the 12-inch MacBook and 2016 MacBook Pro.
Pricing for the new laptop starts at $2899 for the 14-inch model. The 16-inch version starts at $3399.
Pre-orders are available starting today with deliveries starting November 6. You can find the product page for the new MacBook Pro here .
Colors include silver or space black options with standard or nano-texture display configurations.

Beyond the new high-end laptop, Apple also announced the redesigned iPad mini , M6 iMac , and M6 14-inch MacBook Pro this week. Back in March, Apple upgraded the standard 14- and 16-inch MacBook Pro laptops to the current M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.
Apple calls the new design both thinner and lighter than the standard MacBook Pro models in the same size configuration.
The new MacBook Pros look awesome with glowing Apple logos. We’re so back. pic.twitter.com/Ce6G8EIVQF
The new MacBook Pro is the first to use what Apple calls a PROLED XDR display, replacing Mini-LED as the MacBook Pro display technology.

While Apple has innovated with multi-touch on the iPhone and iPad, the Mac has been resistant to touch input for years. The new MacBook Pro changes that with the first touchscreen Mac display. Here’s what Apple says about touch on the Mac.

MacBook Pro features Touch for the first time, bringing pros a whole new way to interact with their content. Crafted specifically for the Mac, every touch interaction feels incredibly responsive and refined. Everyday tasks are simple and intuitive, allowing users to scroll through a webpage with a natural swipe; pinch to zoom in on a photo; drag and drop slides from one presentation to another; and double-tap a window to fill the screen, or flick to tile it into place. And the touch sensor is built directly into the display panel — not layered on top of it — reducing latency so users feel like they’re touching the content itself.
Apple also touts the use of a new hinge technology in the MacBook Pro, in part to support touch input without compromising on stability:

Touch also introduces entirely new ways of working for pro users. Graphic designers can now use the entire display as their canvas, no longer constrained by the area of the trackpad when drawing; musicians can play software instruments right onscreen; and app developers can test how Touch performs in their iOS and iPadOS apps directly on the MacBook Pro display. And these new ways to interact with MacBook Pro work in tandem with the keyboard shortcuts and trackpad gestures pros know and love. In addition, a newly designed hinge provides greater stability while using Touch, and advanced video stabilization automatically smooths the camera feed in real time while using Touch on a video call.
In addition to touch as an additional input method, the new MacBook Pro also adopts the Dynamic Island in favor of the notch.
The Dynamic Island now comes to Mac, serving as the home for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI.

Not interested in touch? The existing MacBook Pro configurations from March stick around at the same prices. You just lose OLED, the glowing Apple logo, and the thinner and lighter design. Performance, however, is pretty much on par between versions as both offer M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.
The new laptops can be configured with up to 128GB of unified memory and 16TB of solid state drive storage.
Peak display brightness jumps from 1600 nits to 2000 nits for HDR content.

I honestly think this is a downgrade. Remember when Apple introduced the Touch Bar? It was supposed to be a big deal, but eventually Apple removed it. Now they’re adding a touchscreen to the MacBook. What’s the actual point?

If it supported the Apple Pencil, I could understand the appeal, especially for designers. But without it, I honestly don’t see much use for it. Maybe I’m wrong, but I’ve used touchscreen Windows laptops before, and I never really found it useful.

I can’t help wondering whether Steve Jobs would have approved of this direction. Apple needs a better marketing team that understands what people actually want, rather than adding a touchscreen that, in my opinion, offers very little practical use.

The 14-inch model is half a pound lighter at just 3 pounds even compared to 3.5 pounds for the same version of the previous design. The overall footprint is reduced as well with 0.59 x 12.24 x 8.52 inch dimensions compared to 0.61 x 12.31 x 8.71 inch dimensions when comparing 14-inch models.

The 16-inch model is notably lighter as well. The new design weighs in at 4 pounds even compared to 4.7 pounds for the previous design. Dimensions change to 0.63 x 14 x 9.62 inches compared to 0.66 x 14.01 x 9.77 inches between designs.
Playing piano on the touchscreen MacBook Pro pic.twitter.com/lDlwIeqErd

The new machines still use Touch ID with no Face ID support. Apple also doesn’t offer built-in cellular models of the new MacBook Pro. We’ll have to keep waiting for Face ID and built-in cellular connectivity.
You can find Apple’s press release for the new machines here .

sources.title: Apple announces touchscreen MacBook Pro with OLED display
passages: LOS ANGELES—Apple today announced and gave a first glimpse of its first major MacBook Pro redesign in more than five years.
As rumored, it includes an OLED display and, for the first time on macOS, a touchscreen—a change Apple has long debated. (Former CEO Steve Jobs famously was opposed.)

The OLED display (which Apple is, of course, calling the PROLED XDR) seems to be the real highlight here, compared to earlier models: It can achieve 2,000 nits in terms of maximum brightness, and Apple says it has a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio.
References were made to burn-in protection, but details on which approach it’s taking for that weren’t yet shared.
The display retains the 120 Hz variable refresh rate of its predecessors.
Beyond that, the design is largely similar to the existing one, but there are a few notable differences.
Apple said when announcing it that the 14-inch model is just 3 pounds, down around half a pound from the previous model, depending on configuration.
Memory configurations top out where they did in previous MacBook Pro models with M5 Max: up to 128GB of RAM.
That said, storage can now go up to 16TB—if you can afford it.
Apple’s demonstration video showed users interacting with applications by reaching up to touch the screen, including file dragging and multi-touch gestures like pinch-to-zoom.

The M6 series has already arrived in other Macs, but it seems Apple is skipping them for this refresh; there were previously reports that Apple planned to hold off on updating the chip until the M7 series, which could have significant improvements for AI performance, just like the recently released A20 Pro chip for the iPhone does.
Second, the top-of-screen camera notch has been replaced by the small black cutout that Apple calls the Dynamic Island.
Presumably it works similarly to the one we’ve seen on the iPhone, expanding or contracting to show live activities and other information.
Finally, there’s a retro throwback: The Apple logo on the back of the lid glows like the logo on MacBooks of yore.

extraction.body: Apple has officially introduced the all-new MacBook Pro, marking a major milestone as the company's first touchscreen Mac. Powered by the M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, this high-end laptop features a completely redesigned, thinner, and lighter form factor alongside cutting-edge display technology. The headline feature is the PROLED XDR display, which replaces previous Mini-LED panels with tandem OLED technology. This upgrade increases peak HDR brightness to 2000 nits and introduces intuitive touch capabilities to the macOS ecosystem for the first time. The physical design also revives the classic light-up Apple logo on the exterior lid. The 14-inch model weighs 3 pounds with dimensions of 0.59 x 12.24 x 8.52 inches, while the 16-inch model weighs 4 pounds with dimensions of 0.63 x 14 x 9.62 inches. Biometric security continues to rely on Touch ID, as Face ID and built-in cellular connectivity are not included in this release. Available in silver and space black, finishes can be paired with standard or nano-texture display options. Pre-orders are open immediately, with official deliveries scheduled to begin on November 6.
