extraction.body: It's almost here! Apple's annual September event is right around the corner, although it will certainly look a little different this year and might not include one of the major products we expect to see each year at this time. This week also saw new rumors about iPhone 12 launch plans, new developments in the dispute between Apple and Epic Games, and a rumor about the chip destined for the first Apple Silicon-based Mac. Read on below for all of the details on next Tuesday's event and more! Apple on Tuesday announced that it will be holding a digital-only media event on Tuesday, September 15 , with the event being streamed from the company's Apple Park headquarters. While September is the traditional time for Apple's iPhone event, reliable sources are indicating that we will NOT be seeing the introduction of the iPhone 12 lineup at next week's event. Instead, the event with a tagline of "Time Flies" will be largely focused on new Apple Watch and iPad models . Check out our complete look at what we expect to see at the event for more details. Apple's event page includes an animated augmented reality logo that you can place in the real world, while just ahead of the event announcement Twitter debuted a custom hashflag Apple icon for those using the #appleevent hashtag. If the iPhone 12 isn't coming at next week's event, when can we expect it? Apple has said the new iPhones will be launching "a few weeks later" than usual, so another event in early October seems likely. But even then, word is that the four new iPhone 12 models will see a staggered launch due to supply constraints. Most reports have suggested the 5.4-inch and 6.1-inch iPhone 12 models would launch first, with the 6.1-inch and 6.7-inch iPhone 12 Pro models coming a bit later, but a new report claims that it will be the two 6.1-inch models (one regular and one Pro) launching first . Regardless of the exact timing, carriers are starting to ramp up preparations for the launch, and Apple is said to be starting mass production on the new models later this month . One of the key features of the iPhone 12 lineup will be 5G support, but not all models will have the same types of 5G support, so check out our guide to mmWave vs. Sub-6GHz 5G to learn about the differences. Yes, the war between Apple and Epic Games continues to rage, with Epic last weekend asking a court to force Apple to reinstate Epic's developer account and put Fortnite back on the App Store . Epic says it is "likely to suffer irreparable harm" if Fortnite is kept off of the App Store. For its part, Apple says that the situation is of Epic's own making, and Apple has filed a countersuit for breach of contract damages. Apple says Epic engaged in "willful, brazen, and unlawful conduct" in what amounts to "nothing more than a basic disagreement over money." That obviously didn't sit well with Epic founder and CEO Tim Sweeney, who shared a Twitter thread arguing that Apple has "lost sight of the tech industry's founding principles" and that the rights of users and creators are the foundation of Epic's actions and lawsuit. Apple has said that its first Macs using Apple-designed processors will launch before the end of the year, and a new report claims that an A14X chip destined for both the first Apple Silicon Mac and an updated iPad Pro will be entering production in the fourth quarter of this year. A previous rumor claimed that the first Apple Silicon Mac will be a revived 12-inch MacBook sporting battery life of 15-20 hours and based on TSMC's latest 5-nanometer chip process for maximum efficiency. Apple is famous for disguising its prototype devices to make it more difficult to identify them, and some new photos reveal the lengths Apple went to in hiding the Apple Watch before its debut . The photos reveal the Apple Watch hidden inside a protective case that resembles an iPod nano, which is fitting considering that in the days before the Apple Watch, some iPod nano owners took to wearing their devices as wristwatches using third-party cases. But even then, word is that the four new iPhone 12 models will see a staggered launch due to supply constraints. Most reports have suggested the 5.4-inch and 6.1-inch iPhone 12 models would launch first, with the 6.1-inch and 6.7-inch iPhone 12 Pro models coming a bit later, but a new report claims that it will be the two 6.1-inch models (one regular and one Pro) launching first .
Regardless of the exact timing, carriers are starting to ramp up preparations for the launch, and Apple is said to be starting mass production on the new models later this month .

One of the key features of the iPhone 12 lineup will be 5G support, but not all models will have the same types of 5G support, so check out our guide to mmWave vs. Sub-6GHz 5G to learn about the differences.

Yes, the war between Apple and Epic Games continues to rage, with Epic last weekend asking a court to force Apple to reinstate Epic's developer account and put Fortnite back on the App Store . Epic says it is "likely to suffer irreparable harm" if Fortnite is kept off of the App Store.

For its part, Apple says that the situation is of Epic's own making, and Apple has filed a countersuit for breach of contract damages. Apple says Epic engaged in "willful, brazen, and unlawful conduct" in what amounts to "nothing more than a basic disagreement over money."

That obviously didn't sit well with Epic founder and CEO Tim Sweeney, who shared a Twitter thread arguing that Apple has "lost sight of the tech industry's founding principles" and that the rights of users and creators are the foundation of Epic's actions and lawsuit.

Apple has said that its first Macs using Apple-designed processors will launch before the end of the year, and a new report claims that an A14X chip destined for both the first Apple Silicon Mac and an updated iPad Pro will be entering production in the fourth quarter of this year.

A previous rumor claimed that the first Apple Silicon Mac will be a revived 12-inch MacBook sporting battery life of 15-20 hours and based on TSMC's latest 5-nanometer chip process for maximum efficiency.
Apple is famous for disguising its prototype devices to make it more difficult to identify them, and some new photos reveal the lengths Apple went to in hiding the Apple Watch before its debut .

The photos reveal the Apple Watch hidden inside a protective case that resembles an iPod nano, which is fitting considering that in the days before the Apple Watch, some iPod nano owners took to wearing their devices as wristwatches using third-party cases.

extraction.body: Apple once scoffed at the idea of a laptop with a touchscreen. But that all changed on Wednesday when the tech giant announced the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, its first laptop with a touch-sensitive display. For years, PC makers have been releasing touchscreen computers in an attempt to modernize laptops for the mobile era. Apple is late to the game, but is betting its touchscreen laptop will appeal to the MacBook Pro’s core audience of creative professionals and app developers. Today’s announcement marks the latest in a blitz of new Apple products to launch during John Ternus’ first two months as the company’s CEO. The touchscreen MacBook – along with other Apple firsts like the iPhone Duo and HomeView home hub – will test whether Apple can still develop hit products that anticipate users’ needs. Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook The new touchscreen MacBook Pro, which launches on November 6, will come in 14-inch and 16-inch versions and runs on Apple’s M5 Pro or M5 Max chips. The smaller model starts at $2,899, the bigger at $3,399. Apple is touting the touchscreen as being useful for dragging and dropping slides between presentations, allowing developers to directly test on their computers how their apps work. It also highlighted its usefulness for graphic designers and musicians, saying they’ll be able to draw sketches and play virtual instruments with just a touch of the screen. The company also claims many existing apps will work with the touchscreen right away because the software will register touches as clicks. The Dynamic Island, or the pill-shaped carveout topping iPhone screens with information and the front camera, will also be included on the new laptop. The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display also includes additions aimed at creatives, like higher peak brightness than non-touch versions and Adobe’s RGB color space. The company says the touch sensor is built into the display itself rather than layered on top of it, which it claims will reduce latency when swiping and scrolling. Struggles of early touchscreen laptops Touchscreen laptops have existed for more than a decade. Microsoft made a major push to shift the industry in this direction with the release of Windows 8 in 2012. That software featured a new design with larger tile-shaped icons meant to resemble phones and tablets. The hardware also needed work; early touchscreen laptops were clunky, expensive and awkward to use as tablets. PC makers struggled to keep pace with the rise of smartphones and tablets. “Our competition is different, they’re confused,” Tim Cook, Apple’s then-CEO who is now executive chair of its board of directors, said during a 2013 event. He said rival laptop makers were trying to “make PCs into tablets and tablets into PCs. Who knows what they will do next?” Despite those early gripes, touchscreen laptops have improved over the years thanks to lower component costs, lighter designs and enhancements to Windows. Even Apple, which previously criticized hybrid computers, has been inching in its products in this direction for years. It overhauled the iPad’s software in 2019 with more productivity features, like the ability to use more than one app at once. Yet touchscreen devices only accounted for 16.3% of global laptop shipments in 2025, according to market research from the International Data Corporation. That’s largely because touchscreens aren’t popular with commercial buyers since most workers just plug their laptop into a monitor when they’re at their desk, according to Ryan Reith, group vice president for the IDC. Apple previously tried incorporating touch technology into the MacBook Pro in 2016 with the introduction of the Touch Bar, a touch-sensitive strip located above the keyboard for accessing app controls and other shortcuts. But it largely flopped with consumers because its utility didn’t justify the additional cost. Apple’s next era Apple is known for being late to technologies – usually for good reason. It wasn’t the first company to launch MP3 players, tablets or smartwatches, but it made those products popular with consumers by making its devices simpler and easier to use. The touchscreen MacBook Pro is the latest of several recent examples to follow this playbook. The company introduced its HomeView smart home hub earlier this month, attempting to challenge Amazon’s dominance in the smart home industry. And last week, Apple’s first foldable iPhone went on sale, debuting long after chief rival Samsung established a lead in that market. Apple has long faced pressure to come up with new blockbuster products, especially given Ternus’s background in hardware compared to Cook’s operations expertise. Wall Street will be watching for signs of how Apple’s new products are being received on the company’s earnings call next week, especially following reports of broken iPhone Duo screens. Still, some analysts think Apple’s new laptop will raise the bar for Windows rivals.

coreStoryFacts.text: On top of launching the iPhone Duo this Friday and announcing HomeView just last week, the company has yet another event on its calendar.
The “Pro and tell” event, as teased by Apple SVP of Marketing Greg Joswiak , will be held on October 28 in Los Angeles, where we expect the company to debut its first-ever touchscreen MacBook Pro.
We’ll be covering everything that Apple announces during its event next week, so keep it locked to The Shortcut and be sure to subscribe if you haven’t already.
Elsewhere, Apple is also expected to announce a new 14-inch MacBook Pro as a new entry-level model with an M6 chip.
It’s not clear if its design will be changing or if there will be a display upgrade, but it sounds like we’ll get an under-the-hood boost nonetheless.
Apple will also reportedly introduce a new iMac powered by the M6 processor.
Apple hasn’t refreshed it since 2024, and this year, it’s set to get one of the biggest upgrades it’s ever gotten with an OLED display.
Some rumors suggest it’ll come with a 120Hz refresh rate, too, which would be killer.
We also anticipate a new chipset and a tweaked design that’s a bit more water resistant.

Apple announced its first touchscreen laptop on October 28, 2026, and the price tag landed as loudly as the feature.
The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display starts at $2,899 for the 14-inch model and $3,399 for the 16-inch, according to Ars Technica’s launch coverage .
Both sizes use Apple’s M5 Pro or M5 Max chips, and both go on sale November 6, 2026.
The gap between the two sizes is exactly $500, or roughly 17% on top of the smaller model’s base price.
Apple has not published a wider configuration list in the material we verified, so those two numbers are the only prices we can state with confidence.
The takeaway: Apple has crossed a line it held for years, and it did so at the top of its price range.
Whether that bet works depends on facts the company has not yet shown, from battery life to repair costs to how well macOS handles fingers.

This analysis covers what Apple confirmed, what it left open, how the pricing compares with the rest of the market, and what the touchscreen MacBook Pro means for buyers, developers and rival laptop makers.
BNN Bloomberg’s report on the first touchscreen laptops arriving amid a product blitz placed the launch inside a busy stretch for Apple, and that context matters for pricing.
When a company launches several products in a short window, it usually prices the newest halo item high and lets cheaper models absorb the volume.
A $2,899 entry point reads as a halo price, aimed at buyers who already pay for top-end Pro hardware.
Investors will watch the November 6 launch window and the following quarter for signs of whether premium Mac demand holds.

Apple calls the product the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, and coverage identifies it as the company’s first laptop with a touch-sensitive screen. It ships in two sizes, 14 inches and 16 inches. Apple’s M5 Pro and M5 Max chips power the lineup. The company showed the machines at its “Pro and tell” event, where John Ternus, identified in coverage as Apple’s CEO, unveiled the touchscreen MacBooks. The headline feature is simple to state. extraction.body: It's almost here! Apple's annual September event is right around the corner, although it will certainly look a little different this year and might not include one of the major products we expect to see each year at this time. This week also saw new rumors about iPhone 12 launch plans, new developments in the dispute between Apple and Epic Games, and a rumor about the chip destined for the first Apple Silicon-based Mac. Read on below for all of the details on next Tuesday's event and more! Apple on Tuesday announced that it will be holding a digital-only media event on Tuesday, September 15 , with the event being streamed from the company's Apple Park headquarters. While September is the traditional time for Apple's iPhone event, reliable sources are indicating that we will NOT be seeing the introduction of the iPhone 12 lineup at next week's event. Instead, the event with a tagline of "Time Flies" will be largely focused on new Apple Watch and iPad models . Check out our complete look at what we expect to see at the event for more details. Apple's event page includes an animated augmented reality logo that you can place in the real world, while just ahead of the event announcement Twitter debuted a custom hashflag Apple icon for those using the #appleevent hashtag. If the iPhone 12 isn't coming at next week's event, when can we expect it? Apple has said the new iPhones will be launching "a few weeks later" than usual, so another event in early October seems likely. But even then, word is that the four new iPhone 12 models will see a staggered launch due to supply constraints. Most reports have suggested the 5.4-inch and 6.1-inch iPhone 12 models would launch first, with the 6.1-inch and 6.7-inch iPhone 12 Pro models coming a bit later, but a new report claims that it will be the two 6.1-inch models (one regular and one Pro) launching first . Regardless of the exact timing, carriers are starting to ramp up preparations for the launch, and Apple is said to be starting mass production on the new models later this month . One of the key features of the iPhone 12 lineup will be 5G support, but not all models will have the same types of 5G support, so check out our guide to mmWave vs. Sub-6GHz 5G to learn about the differences. Yes, the war between Apple and Epic Games continues to rage, with Epic last weekend asking a court to force Apple to reinstate Epic's developer account and put Fortnite back on the App Store . Epic says it is "likely to suffer irreparable harm" if Fortnite is kept off of the App Store. For its part, Apple says that the situation is of Epic's own making, and Apple has filed a countersuit for breach of contract damages. Apple says Epic engaged in "willful, brazen, and unlawful conduct" in what amounts to "nothing more than a basic disagreement over money." That obviously didn't sit well with Epic founder and CEO Tim Sweeney, who shared a Twitter thread arguing that Apple has "lost sight of the tech industry's founding principles" and that the rights of users and creators are the foundation of Epic's actions and lawsuit. Apple has said that its first Macs using Apple-designed processors will launch before the end of the year, and a new report claims that an A14X chip destined for both the first Apple Silicon Mac and an updated iPad Pro will be entering production in the fourth quarter of this year. A previous rumor claimed that the first Apple Silicon Mac will be a revived 12-inch MacBook sporting battery life of 15-20 hours and based on TSMC's latest 5-nanometer chip process for maximum efficiency. Apple is famous for disguising its prototype devices to make it more difficult to identify them, and some new photos reveal the lengths Apple went to in hiding the Apple Watch before its debut . The photos reveal the Apple Watch hidden inside a protective case that resembles an iPod nano, which is fitting considering that in the days before the Apple Watch, some iPod nano owners took to wearing their devices as wristwatches using third-party cases. passages: It's almost here! Apple's annual September event is right around the corner, although it will certainly look a little different this year and might not include one of the major products we expect to see each year at this time.
This week also saw new rumors about iPhone 12 launch plans, new developments in the dispute between Apple and Epic Games, and a rumor about the chip destined for the first Apple Silicon-based Mac.
Read on below for all of the details on next Tuesday's event and more!
Apple on Tuesday announced that it will be holding a digital-only media event on Tuesday, September 15 , with the event being streamed from the company's Apple Park headquarters.

While September is the traditional time for Apple's iPhone event, reliable sources are indicating that we will NOT be seeing the introduction of the iPhone 12 lineup at next week's event. Instead, the event with a tagline of "Time Flies" will be largely focused on new Apple Watch and iPad models . Check out our complete look at what we expect to see at the event for more details.

Apple's event page includes an animated augmented reality logo that you can place in the real world, while just ahead of the event announcement Twitter debuted a custom hashflag Apple icon for those using the #appleevent hashtag.

If the iPhone 12 isn't coming at next week's event, when can we expect it? Apple has said the new iPhones will be launching "a few weeks later" than usual, so another event in early October seems likely.

But even then, word is that the four new iPhone 12 models will see a staggered launch due to supply constraints. Most reports have suggested the 5.4-inch and 6.1-inch iPhone 12 models would launch first, with the 6.1-inch and 6.7-inch iPhone 12 Pro models coming a bit later, but a new report claims that it will be the two 6.1-inch models (one regular and one Pro) launching first .
Regardless of the exact timing, carriers are starting to ramp up preparations for the launch, and Apple is said to be starting mass production on the new models later this month .

One of the key features of the iPhone 12 lineup will be 5G support, but not all models will have the same types of 5G support, so check out our guide to mmWave vs. Sub-6GHz 5G to learn about the differences.

Yes, the war between Apple and Epic Games continues to rage, with Epic last weekend asking a court to force Apple to reinstate Epic's developer account and put Fortnite back on the App Store . Epic says it is "likely to suffer irreparable harm" if Fortnite is kept off of the App Store.

For its part, Apple says that the situation is of Epic's own making, and Apple has filed a countersuit for breach of contract damages. Apple says Epic engaged in "willful, brazen, and unlawful conduct" in what amounts to "nothing more than a basic disagreement over money."

That obviously didn't sit well with Epic founder and CEO Tim Sweeney, who shared a Twitter thread arguing that Apple has "lost sight of the tech industry's founding principles" and that the rights of users and creators are the foundation of Epic's actions and lawsuit.

Apple has said that its first Macs using Apple-designed processors will launch before the end of the year, and a new report claims that an A14X chip destined for both the first Apple Silicon Mac and an updated iPad Pro will be entering production in the fourth quarter of this year.

A previous rumor claimed that the first Apple Silicon Mac will be a revived 12-inch MacBook sporting battery life of 15-20 hours and based on TSMC's latest 5-nanometer chip process for maximum efficiency.
Apple is famous for disguising its prototype devices to make it more difficult to identify them, and some new photos reveal the lengths Apple went to in hiding the Apple Watch before its debut .

The photos reveal the Apple Watch hidden inside a protective case that resembles an iPod nano, which is fitting considering that in the days before the Apple Watch, some iPod nano owners took to wearing their devices as wristwatches using third-party cases.

sources.title: Apple just announced its first ever MacBook with a touchscreen
passages: The touchscreen MacBook – along with other Apple firsts like the iPhone Duo and HomeView home hub – will test whether Apple can still develop hit products that anticipate users’ needs.
Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook The new touchscreen MacBook Pro, which launches on November 6, will come in 14-inch and 16-inch versions and runs on Apple’s M5 Pro or M5 Max chips.
Apple once scoffed at the idea of a laptop with a touchscreen.
Apple is late to the game, but is betting its touchscreen laptop will appeal to the MacBook Pro’s core audience of creative professionals and app developers.
Today’s announcement marks the latest in a blitz of new Apple products to launch during John Ternus’ first two months as the company’s CEO.
“Our competition is different, they’re confused,” Tim Cook, Apple’s then-CEO who is now executive chair of its board of directors, said during a 2013 event.
Apple is touting the touchscreen as being useful for dragging and dropping slides between presentations, allowing developers to directly test on their computers how their apps work.
Apple has long faced pressure to come up with new blockbuster products, especially given Ternus’s background in hardware compared to Cook’s operations expertise.
Still, some analysts think Apple’s new laptop will raise the bar for Windows rivals.

extraction.body: Apple once scoffed at the idea of a laptop with a touchscreen. But that all changed on Wednesday when the tech giant announced the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, its first laptop with a touch-sensitive display. For years, PC makers have been releasing touchscreen computers in an attempt to modernize laptops for the mobile era. Apple is late to the game, but is betting its touchscreen laptop will appeal to the MacBook Pro’s core audience of creative professionals and app developers. Today’s announcement marks the latest in a blitz of new Apple products to launch during John Ternus’ first two months as the company’s CEO. The touchscreen MacBook – along with other Apple firsts like the iPhone Duo and HomeView home hub – will test whether Apple can still develop hit products that anticipate users’ needs. Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook The new touchscreen MacBook Pro, which launches on November 6, will come in 14-inch and 16-inch versions and runs on Apple’s M5 Pro or M5 Max chips. The smaller model starts at $2,899, the bigger at $3,399. Apple is touting the touchscreen as being useful for dragging and dropping slides between presentations, allowing developers to directly test on their computers how their apps work. It also highlighted its usefulness for graphic designers and musicians, saying they’ll be able to draw sketches and play virtual instruments with just a touch of the screen. The company also claims many existing apps will work with the touchscreen right away because the software will register touches as clicks. The Dynamic Island, or the pill-shaped carveout topping iPhone screens with information and the front camera, will also be included on the new laptop. The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display also includes additions aimed at creatives, like higher peak brightness than non-touch versions and Adobe’s RGB color space. The company says the touch sensor is built into the display itself rather than layered on top of it, which it claims will reduce latency when swiping and scrolling. Struggles of early touchscreen laptops Touchscreen laptops have existed for more than a decade. Microsoft made a major push to shift the industry in this direction with the release of Windows 8 in 2012. That software featured a new design with larger tile-shaped icons meant to resemble phones and tablets. The hardware also needed work; early touchscreen laptops were clunky, expensive and awkward to use as tablets. PC makers struggled to keep pace with the rise of smartphones and tablets. “Our competition is different, they’re confused,” Tim Cook, Apple’s then-CEO who is now executive chair of its board of directors, said during a 2013 event. He said rival laptop makers were trying to “make PCs into tablets and tablets into PCs. Who knows what they will do next?” Despite those early gripes, touchscreen laptops have improved over the years thanks to lower component costs, lighter designs and enhancements to Windows. Even Apple, which previously criticized hybrid computers, has been inching in its products in this direction for years. It overhauled the iPad’s software in 2019 with more productivity features, like the ability to use more than one app at once. Yet touchscreen devices only accounted for 16.3% of global laptop shipments in 2025, according to market research from the International Data Corporation. That’s largely because touchscreens aren’t popular with commercial buyers since most workers just plug their laptop into a monitor when they’re at their desk, according to Ryan Reith, group vice president for the IDC. Apple previously tried incorporating touch technology into the MacBook Pro in 2016 with the introduction of the Touch Bar, a touch-sensitive strip located above the keyboard for accessing app controls and other shortcuts. But it largely flopped with consumers because its utility didn’t justify the additional cost. Apple’s next era Apple is known for being late to technologies – usually for good reason. It wasn’t the first company to launch MP3 players, tablets or smartwatches, but it made those products popular with consumers by making its devices simpler and easier to use. The touchscreen MacBook Pro is the latest of several recent examples to follow this playbook. The company introduced its HomeView smart home hub earlier this month, attempting to challenge Amazon’s dominance in the smart home industry. And last week, Apple’s first foldable iPhone went on sale, debuting long after chief rival Samsung established a lead in that market. Apple has long faced pressure to come up with new blockbuster products, especially given Ternus’s background in hardware compared to Cook’s operations expertise. Wall Street will be watching for signs of how Apple’s new products are being received on the company’s earnings call next week, especially following reports of broken iPhone Duo screens. Still, some analysts think Apple’s new laptop will raise the bar for Windows rivals.

passages: Critiques of the SECURE Data Act assume that stronger-sounding provisions necessarily produce better outcomes.
Critics point to its less restrictive data minimization framework, lack of a private right of action, and preemption of state laws as provisions that will fail to adequately protect consumers.
For decades, the United States has relied on a patchwork of sector-specific and state laws to govern data privacy.
Data collection is not inherently harmful to consumers; in fact, many forms of data collection benefit consumers by improving the services Americans rely on every day.
That translates to more personalized health care, more efficient energy usage, and more reliable transportation.
This approach mimics the vast majority of state privacy laws in both red and blue states.

The debate over federal privacy legislation should not center on whether Congress can produce the most restrictive possible framework, but whether it can establish a workable national standard that meaningfully protects consumers while preserving the benefits of data-driven innovation.

Rather than restarting debates that have repeatedly prevented federal action, Congress should build on this emerging consensus and finally provide Americans with a consistent national privacy framework.
These provisions have been adopted in states led by both Democrats and Republicans, reflecting an emerging consensus around a balanced approach to privacy governance.
Private rights of action lead to fragmented interpretations and opportunistic litigation disconnected from concrete consumer harm.
Centralized enforcement, on the other hand, promotes consistency, provides expert oversight, deters bad actors, and allows regulators to focus on meaningful violations.

extraction.body: For decades, the United States has relied on a patchwork of sector-specific and state laws to govern data privacy. Various attempts at comprehensive federal privacy legislation have stalled in Congress, largely due to conflict on key issues, including federal preemption and a private right of action. The House Financial Services Committee and House Energy and Commerce Committee announced a joint effort in April to advance a new privacy bill, the SECURE Data Act . While this bill would preempt state privacy laws, it also draws heavily from those laws, reflecting a bipartisan, multistate consensus on key privacy provisions that would protect consumers while enabling innovation that bolsters the U.S. economy. Critiques of the SECURE Data Act assume that stronger-sounding provisions necessarily produce better outcomes. Critics point to its less restrictive data minimization framework, lack of a private right of action, and preemption of state laws as provisions that will fail to adequately protect consumers. Furthermore, the SECURE Data Act was the result of a “ unified House Republican effort ,” but gaining Democrats’ support remains a key barrier to the bill’s passage, and these provisions will likely be the biggest sticking points. However, looking to state privacy laws proves critics’ assumptions wrong and presents a path forward for the SECURE DATA Act, both on the merits of the bill and its political appeal. First, the SECURE Data Act avoids importing the more restrictive data minimization framework of the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which even European policymakers admit needs reform . Data collection is not inherently harmful to consumers; in fact, many forms of data collection benefit consumers by improving the services Americans rely on every day. That translates to more personalized health care, more efficient energy usage, and more reliable transportation. The SECURE Data Act preserves more of these beneficial use cases while still giving consumers more control over their data. This approach mimics the vast majority of state privacy laws in both red and blue states. Second, the SECURE Data Act’s reliance on the FTC and state attorneys general for enforcement reflects the most effective approach to complex, economy-wide regulatory frameworks. Private rights of action lead to fragmented interpretations and opportunistic litigation disconnected from concrete consumer harm. Centralized enforcement, on the other hand, promotes consistency, provides expert oversight, deters bad actors, and allows regulators to focus on meaningful violations. Finally, by preempting state privacy laws, the SECURE Data Act creates a uniform national standard that reduces compliance fragmentation while preserving core consumer protections and incentivizing responsible data use. Rather than revisiting proposals that failed to achieve legislative consensus at the state level, the SECURE Data Act closely tracks the model enacted in multiple states across the political spectrum, consolidating state innovation into a workable consensus. As figure 1 illustrates, 21 states have enacted privacy laws with provisions similar to the SECURE Data Act. These provisions have been adopted in states led by both Democrats and Republicans, reflecting an emerging consensus around a balanced approach to privacy governance. The debate over federal privacy legislation should not center on whether Congress can produce the most restrictive possible framework, but whether it can establish a workable national standard that meaningfully protects consumers while preserving the benefits of data-driven innovation. The SECURE Data Act reflects the direction many states have already taken: stronger consumer protections, clear rules for businesses, centralized enforcement, and flexibility for beneficial data use. Rather than restarting debates that have repeatedly prevented federal action, Congress should build on this emerging consensus and finally provide Americans with a consistent national privacy framework. In practice, the alternative to the SECURE Data Act is not a stronger, perfectly harmonized privacy regime—it is continued fragmentation, rising compliance costs, and weaker national competitiveness. * Figure 1 has been corrected. There are 10 core provisions in the SECURE Data Act, not 11.

extraction.body: Since the passage of the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) in 2018, other U.S. states have followed suit by enacting comprehensive consumer data privacy laws in rapid succession. While these state consumer privacy laws tend to have similar themes and address comparable topics, there are also important differences among them — meaning a one-size-fits-all data privacy program will not suffice. Given that the federal government has yet to pass a comprehensive consumer data privacy law, organizations must ensure they comply with the law of each applicable state and monitor this rapidly evolving regulatory environment. For a summary comparison of U.S. state comprehensive consumer data privacy laws enacted as of January 15, 2026 , download Foley’s U.S. State Comprehensive Consumer Data Privacy Law Comparison Chart . Because this chart does not cover every aspect of each state law, it should be used for informational purposes only. Considering the growing pressure on business leaders to protect the confidentiality, integrity and availability of personally identifiable information ( PII ), it is increasingly important that CISOs, CIOs and other IT leaders are aware of and conform to the requirements specified in that legislation. Its enforcement actions protect consumers from unfair or deceptive practices and impose federal privacy and data protection regulations . In addition, more than half of U.S. states have proposed or passed some form of targeted legislation citing the use of AI in political campaigns, schooling, crime data, sexual offenses and deepfakes. California has been the leader in data privacy legislation, enacting more laws than any other state. The California Consumer Privacy Act ( CCPA ) has been in effect since 2020. It specifies that residents can ask businesses to disclose the type of information they collect, why they're collecting the information and the source of the data. The California Privacy Rights Act, in effect since 2023, amends and builds on CCPA by giving residents the ability to prevent businesses from sharing their personal data, request that personal data inaccuracies be corrected, and prevent companies from using sensitive PII, such as race and sexual preference. The Colorado Privacy Act, in effect since 2023, grants consumers rights to manage their personal data and specifies how businesses must protect personal data . Colorado was the first state to enact a broad-based regulation on AI usage, known as the Colorado Artificial Intelligence Act. Passed in 2024 and going into effect in 2026, it will require AI systems developers "to use reasonable care to protect consumers from any known or reasonably foreseeable risks of algorithmic discrimination in the high-risk system." The Connecticut Data Privacy Act, also known as the Connecticut Personal Data Privacy and Online Monitoring Act, has been in effect since 2023. It specifies consumer rights related to personal data, online monitoring and data privacy. The Delaware Personal Data Privacy Act was signed in 2023 and took effect on Jan. 1, 2025. It outlines consumer rights and business requirements for protecting personal data. The Indiana Consumer Data Protection Act, which goes into effect Jan. 1, 2026, outlines consumer rights and requirements for data protection, including data access, correction and deletion, and the ability to opt out of targeted advertising. The Montana Consumer Data Privacy Act, in effect since 2024 and amended in April 2025, applies to entities that conduct business in Montana or provide products or services to Montana residents. The Nebraska Data Privacy Act, which went into effect on Jan. 1, 2025, addresses key aspects of data privacy and protection for businesses that do business in Nebraska or its residents, or process or sell personal data. The New Hampshire Privacy Act took effect on Jan. 1, 2025. It applies to entities that conduct business in New Hampshire or create products or services targeting New Hampshire residents. The Texas Data Privacy and Security Act went into effect in 2024. The Utah Consumer Privacy Act has been in effect since 2023. It provides consumer rights and describes business data protection assessments and security measures . The Virginia Consumer Data Protection Act has been in effect since 2023. It grants consumers the right to access, correct, delete and post their personal data; mandates that businesses comply with data protection rules; and affects both government and nongovernment organizations that annually process specific quantities of personal data. extraction.body: Consumer protection enforcement remains a significant risk for businesses in 2026, but the enforcement landscape has shifted considerably. While federal regulators have refocused their attention, including on traditional fraud, deceptive marketing, pricing transparency, subscription programs, and other forms of measurable consumer harm, companies must also contend with growing scrutiny from state Attorneys General (AG) and an increasingly active plaintiffs’ bar. As enforcement priorities continue to evolve, awareness of trends and developments are critical for organizations to reassess their compliance strategies and address emerging risks across advertising, privacy, artificial intelligence, consumer finance, and e-commerce. Members of McDermott Will & Schulte’s cross-practice team discussed how consumer protection enforcement has evolved, and will evolve, during the Trump administration and where businesses face the greatest exposure. Consumer protection enforcement has shifted, not disappeared Under current leadership, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) continues to pursue traditional consumer protection cases involving identifiable deception, fraud, and consumer injury. Rather than developing expansive theories of unfairness, the FTC is increasingly applying longstanding deception principles across industries. Priority areas include pricing transparency, algorithmic pricing, subscriptions and negative options, marketing practices, children’s privacy, artificial intelligence (AI) deceptive marketing, and misleading health claims. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau is operating amid leadership, staffing, and funding uncertainty that have curtailed its enforcement and supervisory activity. However, the agency has not abandoned its statutory mandate, and continues to address traditional fraud, scams targeting vulnerable populations, and cases involving tangible, measurable consumer harm. Businesses should not interpret reduced federal activity as permission to relax existing compliance programs. The underlying statutes remain enforceable, and conduct occurring during a period of reduced scrutiny may still be examined by future agency leadership, state regulators, or private plaintiffs. State AGs are using traditional Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practice statutes, existing and new state privacy laws, industry-specific requirements and, in some cases, federal consumer financial protection authority to investigate conduct across industries. For example, California is increasingly acting as a national enforcement leader, with the AG expanding activity across consumer protection, privacy, and antitrust while federal enforcement recedes. Coordination among states is also becoming more institutionalized. Multistate coalitions, information-sharing agreements, and specialized regulatory groups allow an investigation initiated by one office to expand rapidly. Companies should respond to every regulator inquiry with a potential multistate audience in mind. Subscription practices present similar challenges. Companies should ensure recurring obligations are clearly disclosed, consent is properly obtained, and cancellation is just as easy as enrollment. Dark patterns are also being challenged under both consumer protection and privacy law. Companies should review consent, opt-out, and cancellation flows for equal prominence, comparable steps, and unnecessary friction. Privacy and AI claims are being treated as consumer protection issues Privacy enforcement has not slowed. Regulators are focused on whether companies’ actual practices match their public representations. Privacy policies, cookie banners, settings, and statements such as, “we do not sell your data,” are increasingly treated as advertising claims. Companies should test whether consumer choices work throughout the full technology stack, not merely whether a link or webform exists. Children’s privacy and age assurance are becoming central priorities Children’s privacy is one of the areas where enforcement activity remains particularly strong. Federal Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act requirements now operate alongside a growing number of state laws addressing teen data, age assurance, parental consent, addictive design, targeted advertising, and AI products accessible to minors. The compliance discussion is shifting from whether companies may verify age to whether they have implemented a reasonable age-assurance approach. At the same time, age-verification tools must be designed carefully so that the verification process does not create new privacy risks. Businesses offering services that are directed to, or foreseeably used by, children and teenagers should evaluate: Consumer class action activity continues to rise even as some federal agencies narrow their enforcement posture. Plaintiffs are pursuing claims under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, Fair Credit Reporting Act, Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, and state wiretapping and consumer protection statutes. Plaintiffs’ firms are using regulatory guidance and enforcement actions as litigation roadmaps, particularly in matters involving privacy disclosures, tracking technologies, subscription practices, pricing transparency, dark patterns, and AI marketing. Companies should expect plaintiffs to seek the same internal materials regulators request, including product testing, substantiation records, consumer disclosures, pricing data, cancellation metrics, vendor oversight, and remediation records. The most successful compliance programs will focus on demonstrable consumer harm, clear disclosures, and operational accountability. Companies should develop a consistent, practice-based narrative explaining how the relevant system operates, how it was tested, and what remediation occurred. Inconsistent explanations across jurisdictions can turn a manageable inquiry into a broader credibility problem. Teresa brings a rare end-to-end regulatory perspective shaped by her significant experience at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), where she worked across rulemaking, supervision, enforcement, and litigation. Having operated inside two of the US government’s most powerful consumer financial regulators, Teresa understands not only what the law requires, but how regulators think, prioritize, examine, investigate, and enforce across a wide range of consumer-facing business models. Teresa also advises clients on regulatory, compliance, and enforcement issues related to cryptocurrencies and other digital assets, including consumer-facing crypto products, payments, and emerging blockchain-based business models. At the CFPB, Teresa served in senior roles in the Offices of Regulations, Enforcement, and Supervision. She helped formulate and draft federal consumer financial regulations, advised senior leadership on regulatory strategy, and served as a subject matter expert on key statutes and rules, including the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010, the Electronic Fund Transfer Act of 1978 and Regulation E, and the Truth in Lending Act of 1968 and Regulation Z. She regularly advised examination teams, led and supported challenging supervisory exams, and addressed novel regulatory issues in coordination with enforcement senior staff. passages: Consumer protection enforcement remains a significant risk for businesses in 2026, but the enforcement landscape has shifted considerably. While federal regulators have refocused their attention, including on traditional fraud, deceptive marketing, pricing transparency, subscription programs, and other forms of measurable consumer harm, companies must also contend with growing scrutiny from state Attorneys General (AG) and an increasingly active plaintiffs’ bar. As enforcement priorities continue to evolve, awareness of trends and developments are critical for organizations to reassess their compliance strategies and address emerging risks across advertising, privacy, artificial intelligence, consumer finance, and e-commerce.

Members of McDermott Will & Schulte’s cross-practice team discussed how consumer protection enforcement has evolved, and will evolve, during the Trump administration and where businesses face the greatest exposure.
Consumer protection enforcement has shifted, not disappeared

Under current leadership, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) continues to pursue traditional consumer protection cases involving identifiable deception, fraud, and consumer injury. Rather than developing expansive theories of unfairness, the FTC is increasingly applying longstanding deception principles across industries. Priority areas include pricing transparency, algorithmic pricing, subscriptions and negative options, marketing practices, children’s privacy, artificial intelligence (AI) deceptive marketing, and misleading health claims.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau is operating amid leadership, staffing, and funding uncertainty that have curtailed its enforcement and supervisory activity. However, the agency has not abandoned its statutory mandate, and continues to address traditional fraud, scams targeting vulnerable populations, and cases involving tangible, measurable consumer harm.

Businesses should not interpret reduced federal activity as permission to relax existing compliance programs. The underlying statutes remain enforceable, and conduct occurring during a period of reduced scrutiny may still be examined by future agency leadership, state regulators, or private plaintiffs.

State AGs are using traditional Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practice statutes, existing and new state privacy laws, industry-specific requirements and, in some cases, federal consumer financial protection authority to investigate conduct across industries. For example, California is increasingly acting as a national enforcement leader, with the AG expanding activity across consumer protection, privacy, and antitrust while federal enforcement recedes.

Coordination among states is also becoming more institutionalized. Multistate coalitions, information-sharing agreements, and specialized regulatory groups allow an investigation initiated by one office to expand rapidly. Companies should respond to every regulator inquiry with a potential multistate audience in mind.
Subscription practices present similar challenges. Companies should ensure recurring obligations are clearly disclosed, consent is properly obtained, and cancellation is just as easy as enrollment.

Dark patterns are also being challenged under both consumer protection and privacy law. Companies should review consent, opt-out, and cancellation flows for equal prominence, comparable steps, and unnecessary friction.
Privacy and AI claims are being treated as consumer protection issues
Privacy enforcement has not slowed. Regulators are focused on whether companies’ actual practices match their public representations.
Privacy policies, cookie banners, settings, and statements such as, “we do not sell your data,” are increasingly treated as advertising claims.
Companies should test whether consumer choices work throughout the full technology stack, not merely whether a link or webform exists.
Children’s privacy and age assurance are becoming central priorities

Children’s privacy is one of the areas where enforcement activity remains particularly strong. Federal Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act requirements now operate alongside a growing number of state laws addressing teen data, age assurance, parental consent, addictive design, targeted advertising, and AI products accessible to minors.

The compliance discussion is shifting from whether companies may verify age to whether they have implemented a reasonable age-assurance approach. At the same time, age-verification tools must be designed carefully so that the verification process does not create new privacy risks.
Businesses offering services that are directed to, or foreseeably used by, children and teenagers should evaluate:

Consumer class action activity continues to rise even as some federal agencies narrow their enforcement posture. Plaintiffs are pursuing claims under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, Fair Credit Reporting Act, Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, and state wiretapping and consumer protection statutes.

Plaintiffs’ firms are using regulatory guidance and enforcement actions as litigation roadmaps, particularly in matters involving privacy disclosures, tracking technologies, subscription practices, pricing transparency, dark patterns, and AI marketing.

Companies should expect plaintiffs to seek the same internal materials regulators request, including product testing, substantiation records, consumer disclosures, pricing data, cancellation metrics, vendor oversight, and remediation records.
The most successful compliance programs will focus on demonstrable consumer harm, clear disclosures, and operational accountability. Companies should be able to answer:

This documentation is particularly important in multistate matters. Companies should develop a consistent, practice-based narrative explaining how the relevant system operates, how it was tested, and what remediation occurred. Inconsistent explanations across jurisdictions can turn a manageable inquiry into a broader credibility problem.

Teresa Kosmidis focuses her practice on consumer protection and consumer financial services regulation, compliance, enforcement, and litigation. She advises financial institutions, payments companies, FinTech companies, and other consumer-facing businesses on complex regulatory and enforcement matters at the federal and state levels, including companies that market to consumers, handle payments or billing, or face scrutiny from federal and state regulators.

Teresa brings a rare end-to-end regulatory perspective shaped by her significant experience at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), where she worked across rulemaking, supervision, enforcement, and litigation. Having operated inside two of the US government’s most powerful consumer financial regulators, Teresa understands not only what the law requires, but how regulators think, prioritize, examine, investigate, and enforce across a wide range of consumer-facing business models.

Teresa also advises clients on regulatory, compliance, and enforcement issues related to cryptocurrencies and other digital assets, including consumer-facing crypto products, payments, and emerging blockchain-based business models.

At the CFPB, Teresa served in senior roles in the Offices of Regulations, Enforcement, and Supervision. She helped formulate and draft federal consumer financial regulations, advised senior leadership on regulatory strategy, and served as a subject matter expert on key statutes and rules, including the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010, the Electronic Fund Transfer Act of 1978 and Regulation E, and the Truth in Lending Act of 1968 and Regulation Z. She regularly advised examination teams, led and supported challenging supervisory exams, and addressed novel regulatory issues in coordination with enforcement senior staff.

While at the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, Teresa represented the agency in federal court litigation and investigations involving nonbank financial institutions, including retail and other consumer-facing companies. Her matters included enforcement actions and investigations involving auto finance, payday lending, deceptive marketing and billing practices, and emerging technologies, including Bitcoin-related products. She conducted depositions, managed investigations, and coordinated closely with economists and state regulators.
She also advises clients in connection with transactions, including regulatory due diligence, identifying consumer protection risks, and structuring post-close remediation efforts.

Earlier in her career, Teresa practiced complex commercial litigation at a New York law firm and clerked for the Honorable E. Thomas Boyle of the US District Court for the Eastern District of New York.

With extensive experience guiding companies through matters before US regulators and agencies, Michael has a comprehensive understanding of how investigations and enforcement actions unfold and how best to advocate for clients. He draws on this deep experience in assisting clients with matters before the CFTC, CISA, DOJ, FCC, FINRA, FTC, HHS OCR, NYDFS, SEC, and state attorneys general.

Michael also regularly advises clients on compliance strategies, product design, privacy program development, and risk management with respect to federal and state privacy and data security laws and regulations. He has guided clients through complex issues on an expansive array of counseling matters, including those that involve compliance with CAN-SPAM, COPPA, FCRA, FERPA, the FTC Act, GLBA, HIPAA, NYDFS Part 500, TCPA, and state privacy laws, as well as industry self-regulation on advertising and PCI DSS. Additionally, Michael regularly counsels clients in evaluating and mitigating data-related risks in complex transactions.

Michael frequently contributes to thought leadership on privacy, cybersecurity, and AI legal issues. He has served as the managing editor for the Practising Law Institute’s Privacy Law Answer Book (2023 and 2024 editions). Michael has also co-authored articles in publications including the Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance , the Cybersecurity Law Report , the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Computational Law Report , and the Review of Banking & Financial Services .

coreStoryFacts.text: Critiques of the SECURE Data Act assume that stronger-sounding provisions necessarily produce better outcomes.
Critics point to its less restrictive data minimization framework, lack of a private right of action, and preemption of state laws as provisions that will fail to adequately protect consumers.
For decades, the United States has relied on a patchwork of sector-specific and state laws to govern data privacy.
Data collection is not inherently harmful to consumers; in fact, many forms of data collection benefit consumers by improving the services Americans rely on every day.
That translates to more personalized health care, more efficient energy usage, and more reliable transportation.
This approach mimics the vast majority of state privacy laws in both red and blue states.

The debate over federal privacy legislation should not center on whether Congress can produce the most restrictive possible framework, but whether it can establish a workable national standard that meaningfully protects consumers while preserving the benefits of data-driven innovation.

Rather than restarting debates that have repeatedly prevented federal action, Congress should build on this emerging consensus and finally provide Americans with a consistent national privacy framework.
These provisions have been adopted in states led by both Democrats and Republicans, reflecting an emerging consensus around a balanced approach to privacy governance.
Private rights of action lead to fragmented interpretations and opportunistic litigation disconnected from concrete consumer harm.
Centralized enforcement, on the other hand, promotes consistency, provides expert oversight, deters bad actors, and allows regulators to focus on meaningful violations.
For a summary comparison of U.S. state comprehensive consumer data privacy laws enacted as of January 15, 2026 , download Foley’s U.S.
Because this chart does not cover every aspect of each state law, it should be used for informational purposes only.

Considering the growing pressure on business leaders to protect the confidentiality, integrity and availability of personally identifiable information ( PII ), it is increasingly important that CISOs, CIOs and other IT leaders are aware of and conform to the requirements specified in that legislation.

While no national legislation exists, many U.S. states have enacted their own data privacy laws, including California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Indiana, Iowa, Minnesota, Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Oregon, Tennessee, Texas, Utah and Virginia.
The Federal Trade Commission is a key regulator responsible for assessing compliance with laws that affect data privacy.
Its enforcement actions protect consumers from unfair or deceptive practices and impose federal privacy and data protection regulations .
A notable trend to consider is that businesses operating in multiple states will encounter increased challenges in complying with each state's privacy laws.

While current privacy legislation at state and local levels has evolved into a patchwork of activity, this could well lead to a broad-based bipartisan U.S. national data privacy law that also regulates the development, deployment and application of AI.

extraction.body: For decades, the United States has relied on a patchwork of sector-specific and state laws to govern data privacy. Various attempts at comprehensive federal privacy legislation have stalled in Congress, largely due to conflict on key issues, including federal preemption and a private right of action. The House Financial Services Committee and House Energy and Commerce Committee announced a joint effort in April to advance a new privacy bill, the SECURE Data Act . While this bill would preempt state privacy laws, it also draws heavily from those laws, reflecting a bipartisan, multistate consensus on key privacy provisions that would protect consumers while enabling innovation that bolsters the U.S. economy. Critiques of the SECURE Data Act assume that stronger-sounding provisions necessarily produce better outcomes. Critics point to its less restrictive data minimization framework, lack of a private right of action, and preemption of state laws as provisions that will fail to adequately protect consumers. Furthermore, the SECURE Data Act was the result of a “ unified House Republican effort ,” but gaining Democrats’ support remains a key barrier to the bill’s passage, and these provisions will likely be the biggest sticking points. However, looking to state privacy laws proves critics’ assumptions wrong and presents a path forward for the SECURE DATA Act, both on the merits of the bill and its political appeal. First, the SECURE Data Act avoids importing the more restrictive data minimization framework of the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which even European policymakers admit needs reform . Data collection is not inherently harmful to consumers; in fact, many forms of data collection benefit consumers by improving the services Americans rely on every day. That translates to more personalized health care, more efficient energy usage, and more reliable transportation. The SECURE Data Act preserves more of these beneficial use cases while still giving consumers more control over their data. This approach mimics the vast majority of state privacy laws in both red and blue states. Second, the SECURE Data Act’s reliance on the FTC and state attorneys general for enforcement reflects the most effective approach to complex, economy-wide regulatory frameworks. Private rights of action lead to fragmented interpretations and opportunistic litigation disconnected from concrete consumer harm. Centralized enforcement, on the other hand, promotes consistency, provides expert oversight, deters bad actors, and allows regulators to focus on meaningful violations. Finally, by preempting state privacy laws, the SECURE Data Act creates a uniform national standard that reduces compliance fragmentation while preserving core consumer protections and incentivizing responsible data use. Rather than revisiting proposals that failed to achieve legislative consensus at the state level, the SECURE Data Act closely tracks the model enacted in multiple states across the political spectrum, consolidating state innovation into a workable consensus. As figure 1 illustrates, 21 states have enacted privacy laws with provisions similar to the SECURE Data Act. These provisions have been adopted in states led by both Democrats and Republicans, reflecting an emerging consensus around a balanced approach to privacy governance. The debate over federal privacy legislation should not center on whether Congress can produce the most restrictive possible framework, but whether it can establish a workable national standard that meaningfully protects consumers while preserving the benefits of data-driven innovation. The SECURE Data Act reflects the direction many states have already taken: stronger consumer protections, clear rules for businesses, centralized enforcement, and flexibility for beneficial data use. Rather than restarting debates that have repeatedly prevented federal action, Congress should build on this emerging consensus and finally provide Americans with a consistent national privacy framework. In practice, the alternative to the SECURE Data Act is not a stronger, perfectly harmonized privacy regime—it is continued fragmentation, rising compliance costs, and weaker national competitiveness. * Figure 1 has been corrected. There are 10 core provisions in the SECURE Data Act, not 11.

sources.title: OpenAI plans to buy Google's AI chips, The Information reports - Charlotte Observer
passages: Oct 27 (Reuters) - OpenAI plans to buy Google's AI chips, The Information reported on Tuesday, citing a person familiar with the matter, as technology companies ramp up spending to meet surging demand for AI computing.
OpenAI is already among the largest buyers of Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs), which it uses to train and deploy AI models.
Google began selling TPUs directly to some customers this year.
The reported plan would deepen ties between OpenAI and Alphabet's Google, which compete in AI products and search but have increasingly struck commercial deals.
Last week, OpenAI said it would make its frontier AI models available through Google Cloud.
The report did not disclose financial terms or other details.
Google did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment outside regular business hours, while OpenAI declined to comment.

Alphabet expects to begin recognizing a small percentage of revenue from TPU sales agreements by the end of this year, with the vast majority expected to be recognized in 2027, CFO Anat Ashkenazi previously said.

Amazon, Microsoft and Google parent Alphabet plan to spend as much as $600 billion combined this year on AI infrastructure as investors increasingly question when such spending will translate into meaningful returns.

OpenAI in June unveiled its first custom AI chip designed with Broadcom, and said it planned to deploy the processor by the end of this year as part of a multi-generation chip program. The reported plan would deepen ties between OpenAI and Alphabet Inc's Google, which compete in AI products and search but have increasingly struck commercial deals. Last week, OpenAI said it would make its frontier AI models available through Google Cloud. The report did not disclose financial terms or other details. Google did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment outside regular business hours, while OpenAI declined to comment. Google's tensor processing units (TPUs) have gained traction as an alternative to Nvidia's market-leading GPUs as companies seek cheaper options. Google began selling TPUs directly to some customers this year. Alphabet expects to begin recognizing a small percentage of revenue from TPU sales agreements by the end of this year, with the vast majority expected to be recognized next year, chief financial officer Anat Ashkenazi previously said. “The next generation of AI will require a diverse range of compute,” Google executive Amin Vahdat said in a statement announcing that deal.

The search of a home on Rocky Point Road in Putnam County has resulted in the indictment of one of the 24 people charged this week for their alleged roles in a Sinaloa Cartel-linked drug trafficking organization that distributed large quantities of methamphetamine, fentanyl, cocaine and other drugs in Putnam County and throughout Middle Tennessee. The results of the investigation were initially announced by United States Attorney Braden H. Boucek for the Middle District of Tennessee, and Putnam County Sheriff Eddie Farris later provided additional details. “The allegations in this case are staggering," Boucek said. "A drug trafficking organization with direct ties to the Sinaloa Cartel allegedly moved massive quantities of deadly drugs into our communities, with two of its leaders directing operations from inside Tennessee prisons.” According to a social media post from the sheriff's office, officers from the Putnam County Sheriff’s Office, the Nashville Homeland Security Task Force, and the FBI "executed a search warrant at 8511 Rocky Point Road in Cookeville" on Tuesday, Oct. 27. "As a result of the search warrant in Putnam County, one individual, Roger Dale Floyd, was taken into federal custody," the post reads. "Floyd was arrested and charged with conspiracy to distribute narcotics and distribution of methamphetamine." Floyd, 65, is also known by the nickname of "Crow," according to federal officials. The sheriff's office post notes that in 2025, PCSO "was made aware of a potential drug trafficking organization connected to a Mexican cartel." PCSO's narcotics detective has worked with state and federal officials over the past year on the investigation. "The investigation revealed that the drug trafficking organization was trafficking illegal narcotics into Putnam County from Mexico, with two of the drug trafficking organization’s leaders being incarcerated in Tennessee prisons," the post reads. "Throughout the entire investigation in Middle Tennessee, approximately 500 kilograms of methamphetamine was seized, along with 20 kilograms of fentanyl, 60 kilograms of cocaine, more than $375,000 in cash, multiple firearms, and five vehicles." “I am extremely proud of the dedication and hard work our narcotics detective put into this investigation over the past year," Farris said. "The amount of arrests and amount of drugs seized prove what can be accomplished when local, state and federal law enforcement work together. We will continue working with our state and federal partners to keep dangerous drugs out of Putnam County.” Boucek said, “The Homeland Security Task Force brings together the full strength of our federal, state and local law enforcement partners to dismantle these criminal networks at every level. Let this indictment send a clear message: prison walls and international borders will not shield those who traffic deadly drugs into Middle Tennessee from federal prosecution.” Court documents allege that the organization conspired to distribute hundreds of kilograms of methamphetamine, fentanyl and cocaine while laundering millions of dollars in drug proceeds through financial transactions and bulk cash smuggling to individuals in Mexico responsible for supplying narcotics throughout the United States. “These are not simply drugs being taken off the street, these are dangerous criminal networks being disrupted, resources being taken away from traffickers, and communities being protected,” said Special Agent in Charge Terence G. Reilly of the FBI Nashville Field Office. “This indictment is a result of the efforts of the Nashville Homeland Security Task Force which uses a whole-of-government approach, and represents the power of partnership, combining federal, state and local partners to investigate criminal activity, share intelligence, and hold those responsible accountable. Today’s charges demonstrate that this coordinated strategy is working and our message is clear: justice will find you.” The 33- count indictment, returned by a federal grand jury in Nashville on Oct. 21 and unsealed Oct. 27, charges all 24 defendants with conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute 50 grams or more of methamphetamine, 400 grams or more of fentanyl, five kilograms or more of cocaine, and quantities of heroin and marijuana. The indictment also includes individual drug trafficking charges and firearm offenses against nine defendants. According to court documents, the organization operated under the direction of individuals in Mexico and elsewhere known as “the Office,” who allegedly coordinated drug trafficking activities in the United States on behalf of the Sinaloa Cartel. Humberto Morales, 34, and Jose Martin Perez, 30, both incarcerated in Tennessee Department of Correction facilities on unrelated convictions, allegedly served as high-ranking members who assisted with coordinating and controlling the organization's operations in Middle Tennessee and elsewhere. The organization relied almost exclusively on Signal, an encrypted messaging application, to coordinate drug transactions and avoid law enforcement detection. Customers placed orders through the Office or its representatives, often Morales or Perez, who negotiated prices and arranged delivery locations. The Office then coordinated with couriers and individuals overseeing drug stash houses to facilitate delivery. To evade detection, the organization rotated couriers and vehicles, used vehicles registered to other individuals, exchanged license plates and frequently changed vehicle ownership. When law enforcement encountered or arrested a member, other participants allegedly moved quickly to relocate drugs, firearms and cash from stash houses before officers could take further action. The government is seeking pretrial detention of all 24 defendants, citing danger to the community, risk of flight and potential obstruction of justice. If convicted, Humberto Morales faces a mandatory minimum sentence of 25 years and up to life in federal prison. Each of the remaining 23 defendants faces a mandatory minimum sentence of 10 years and up to life in prison. Your browser is out of date and potentially vulnerable to security risks. extraction.body: Twenty-four individuals have been indicted in a massive drug operation based in Nashville with ties to the Sinaloa Cartel in Mexico, officials announced in a press conference Wednesday. All individuals involved are now federally indicted for moving large quantities of drugs across the United States under orders from cartel leaders in Mexico. Federal officials say two of those leaders, Humberto Morales and Jose Martin Perez, allegedly controlled operations while locked up in Tennessee Department of Correction facilities. The 24 individuals indicted are as follows: Humberto Morales, a/k/a “Pelon,” “Homie,” “Big Homie,” “Jefe,” 34 Jose Martin Perez, a/k/a “JR,” “Junior,” 30 Magdiel Pina Ramirez, a/k/a “Big Show,” “Menique,” “Moises Rojas Rodriguez,” 33 Chason Lipscomb, a/k/a “Kilo,” 29 Roger Dale Floyd, a/k/a “Crow,” 65 Eric Colon, 36 David Joseph Kelsey, 48 Hector Alexis Rodriguez Sanchez, a/k/a “Toly,” 27 Jose Pablo Gachuz-Zamora, 36 Jose Antonio Araujo-Rivas, 32 Montay Batey, 27 Monterrey Batey, 34 Danielle Nuno, 32 Tynerick D. Turner, 26 Reginald Dante Samuels, 37 Jesus Alberto Vazquez Rodriguez, 35 Jose Cano Alonso, a/k/a “Heriberto Alonso Sanchez,” 42 Geovany Jose Rapalo Hernandez, 43 Jose Antonio Olivas-Avila, 22 Juan Ramon Padilla-Torres, 40 Johnny Mason, 33 Quanshala Harper, 30 Cesar Carrillo Polina, 23 Hannah Ireland Thornton, 24 Officers searched multiple locations Tuesday, and the Metro Nashville Police Department booked one of the suspects into the Davidson County Jail. Out of the 24 people indicted, seven were arrested in Nashville, Mt. The remainder of the individuals are already in jail, besides one person who has an active warrant out for their arrest. "This is one of the biggest drug busts I've ever heard of," said Jim Scott, special agent in charge of the Drug Enforcement Administration's Louisville field Division. Items seized in the arrests include: 500 kilograms of methamphetamines 20 kilograms of fentanyl 60 kilograms of cocaine 6 kilograms of marijuana More than $375,000 in cash Firearms Multiple vehicles "These are staggering quantities of drugs, and every kilogram represents drugs that threaten the safety of our community and the lives of our neighbors," United States Attorney for the Middle District of Tennessee Braden Buzek. Officials say the group moved shipments on a weekly basis from September 2025 to September 2026. Officials say which state prisons Morales and Perez operated out of are not available at this time.
