The search of a home on Rocky Point Road in Putnam County has resulted in the indictment of one of the 24 people charged this week for their alleged roles in a Sinaloa Cartel-linked drug trafficking organization that distributed large quantities of methamphetamine, fentanyl, cocaine and other drugs in Putnam County and throughout Middle Tennessee. The results of the investigation were initially announced by United States Attorney Braden H. Boucek for the Middle District of Tennessee, and Putnam County Sheriff Eddie Farris later provided additional details. “The allegations in this case are staggering," Boucek said. "A drug trafficking organization with direct ties to the Sinaloa Cartel allegedly moved massive quantities of deadly drugs into our communities, with two of its leaders directing operations from inside Tennessee prisons.” According to a social media post from the sheriff's office, officers from the Putnam County Sheriff’s Office, the Nashville Homeland Security Task Force, and the FBI "executed a search warrant at 8511 Rocky Point Road in Cookeville" on Tuesday, Oct. 27. "As a result of the search warrant in Putnam County, one individual, Roger Dale Floyd, was taken into federal custody," the post reads. "Floyd was arrested and charged with conspiracy to distribute narcotics and distribution of methamphetamine." Floyd, 65, is also known by the nickname of "Crow," according to federal officials. The sheriff's office post notes that in 2025, PCSO "was made aware of a potential drug trafficking organization connected to a Mexican cartel." PCSO's narcotics detective has worked with state and federal officials over the past year on the investigation. "The investigation revealed that the drug trafficking organization was trafficking illegal narcotics into Putnam County from Mexico, with two of the drug trafficking organization’s leaders being incarcerated in Tennessee prisons," the post reads. "Throughout the entire investigation in Middle Tennessee, approximately 500 kilograms of methamphetamine was seized, along with 20 kilograms of fentanyl, 60 kilograms of cocaine, more than $375,000 in cash, multiple firearms, and five vehicles." “I am extremely proud of the dedication and hard work our narcotics detective put into this investigation over the past year," Farris said. "The amount of arrests and amount of drugs seized prove what can be accomplished when local, state and federal law enforcement work together. We will continue working with our state and federal partners to keep dangerous drugs out of Putnam County.” Boucek said, “The Homeland Security Task Force brings together the full strength of our federal, state and local law enforcement partners to dismantle these criminal networks at every level. Let this indictment send a clear message: prison walls and international borders will not shield those who traffic deadly drugs into Middle Tennessee from federal prosecution.” Court documents allege that the organization conspired to distribute hundreds of kilograms of methamphetamine, fentanyl and cocaine while laundering millions of dollars in drug proceeds through financial transactions and bulk cash smuggling to individuals in Mexico responsible for supplying narcotics throughout the United States. “These are not simply drugs being taken off the street, these are dangerous criminal networks being disrupted, resources being taken away from traffickers, and communities being protected,” said Special Agent in Charge Terence G. Reilly of the FBI Nashville Field Office. “This indictment is a result of the efforts of the Nashville Homeland Security Task Force which uses a whole-of-government approach, and represents the power of partnership, combining federal, state and local partners to investigate criminal activity, share intelligence, and hold those responsible accountable. Today’s charges demonstrate that this coordinated strategy is working and our message is clear: justice will find you.” The 33- count indictment, returned by a federal grand jury in Nashville on Oct. 21 and unsealed Oct. 27, charges all 24 defendants with conspiracy to distribute and possess with intent to distribute 50 grams or more of methamphetamine, 400 grams or more of fentanyl, five kilograms or more of cocaine, and quantities of heroin and marijuana. The indictment also includes individual drug trafficking charges and firearm offenses against nine defendants. According to court documents, the organization operated under the direction of individuals in Mexico and elsewhere known as “the Office,” who allegedly coordinated drug trafficking activities in the United States on behalf of the Sinaloa Cartel. Humberto Morales, 34, and Jose Martin Perez, 30, both incarcerated in Tennessee Department of Correction facilities on unrelated convictions, allegedly served as high-ranking members who assisted with coordinating and controlling the organization's operations in Middle Tennessee and elsewhere. The organization relied almost exclusively on Signal, an encrypted messaging application, to coordinate drug transactions and avoid law enforcement detection. Customers placed orders through the Office or its representatives, often Morales or Perez, who negotiated prices and arranged delivery locations. The Office then coordinated with couriers and individuals overseeing drug stash houses to facilitate delivery. To evade detection, the organization rotated couriers and vehicles, used vehicles registered to other individuals, exchanged license plates and frequently changed vehicle ownership. When law enforcement encountered or arrested a member, other participants allegedly moved quickly to relocate drugs, firearms and cash from stash houses before officers could take further action. The government is seeking pretrial detention of all 24 defendants, citing danger to the community, risk of flight and potential obstruction of justice. If convicted, Humberto Morales faces a mandatory minimum sentence of 25 years and up to life in federal prison. passages: Twenty-four individuals have been indicted in a massive drug operation based in Nashville with ties to the Sinaloa Cartel in Mexico, officials announced in a press conference Wednesday.

Items seized in the arrests include: 500 kilograms of methamphetamines 20 kilograms of fentanyl 60 kilograms of cocaine 6 kilograms of marijuana More than $375,000 in cash Firearms Multiple vehicles "These are staggering quantities of drugs, and every kilogram represents drugs that threaten the safety of our community and the lives of our neighbors," United States Attorney for the Middle District of Tennessee Braden Buzek.

Out of the 24 people indicted, seven were arrested in Nashville, Mt.
This was a joint investigation with the FBI, the Drug Enforcement Administration, IRS criminal investigation, the United States Postal Inspection Service, Homeland Security Investigations, U.S.

extraction.body: Twenty-four individuals have been indicted in a massive drug operation based in Nashville with ties to the Sinaloa Cartel in Mexico, officials announced in a press conference Wednesday. All individuals involved are now federally indicted for moving large quantities of drugs across the United States under orders from cartel leaders in Mexico. Federal officials say two of those leaders, Humberto Morales and Jose Martin Perez, allegedly controlled operations while locked up in Tennessee Department of Correction facilities. The 24 individuals indicted are as follows: Humberto Morales, a/k/a “Pelon,” “Homie,” “Big Homie,” “Jefe,” 34 Jose Martin Perez, a/k/a “JR,” “Junior,” 30 Magdiel Pina Ramirez, a/k/a “Big Show,” “Menique,” “Moises Rojas Rodriguez,” 33 Chason Lipscomb, a/k/a “Kilo,” 29 Roger Dale Floyd, a/k/a “Crow,” 65 Eric Colon, 36 David Joseph Kelsey, 48 Hector Alexis Rodriguez Sanchez, a/k/a “Toly,” 27 Jose Pablo Gachuz-Zamora, 36 Jose Antonio Araujo-Rivas, 32 Montay Batey, 27 Monterrey Batey, 34 Danielle Nuno, 32 Tynerick D. Turner, 26 Reginald Dante Samuels, 37 Jesus Alberto Vazquez Rodriguez, 35 Jose Cano Alonso, a/k/a “Heriberto Alonso Sanchez,” 42 Geovany Jose Rapalo Hernandez, 43 Jose Antonio Olivas-Avila, 22 Juan Ramon Padilla-Torres, 40 Johnny Mason, 33 Quanshala Harper, 30 Cesar Carrillo Polina, 23 Hannah Ireland Thornton, 24 Officers searched multiple locations Tuesday, and the Metro Nashville Police Department booked one of the suspects into the Davidson County Jail. Out of the 24 people indicted, seven were arrested in Nashville, Mt. The remainder of the individuals are already in jail, besides one person who has an active warrant out for their arrest. "This is one of the biggest drug busts I've ever heard of," said Jim Scott, special agent in charge of the Drug Enforcement Administration's Louisville field Division. Items seized in the arrests include: 500 kilograms of methamphetamines 20 kilograms of fentanyl 60 kilograms of cocaine 6 kilograms of marijuana More than $375,000 in cash Firearms Multiple vehicles "These are staggering quantities of drugs, and every kilogram represents drugs that threaten the safety of our community and the lives of our neighbors," United States Attorney for the Middle District of Tennessee Braden Buzek. Officials say the group moved shipments on a weekly basis from September 2025 to September 2026. Officials say which state prisons Morales and Perez operated out of are not available at this time. This was a joint investigation with the FBI, the Drug Enforcement Administration, IRS criminal investigation, the United States Postal Inspection Service, Homeland Security Investigations, U.S. Secret Service, Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, Tennessee Highway Patrol, Tennessee Department of Correction, Putnam County Sheriff's Office, Rutherford County Sheriff's Office, Wilson County Sheriff's Office, Warren County Sheriff's Office, Metropolitan Nashville Police Department and Gwinnett County Sheriff's Office in Georgia.

Combined with the latest long-term expected return outlook, it amounts to JPMorgan signalling to the market that it sees bitcoin not as a short-term volatile asset but as one of the targets for long-term asset allocation.The point to watch is whether actual fund flows will follow the outlook.

Matt Hougan (맷 호건), chief investment officer at Bitwise, said JPMorgan has moved from a sceptical stance on bitcoin to a stage where it is releasing long-term performance projections.JPMorgan cited expanding capital expenditure worldwide as the backdrop for the outlook.
JPMorgan said investors still view gold more optimistically than bitcoin.

It said a $15 trillion global capital expenditure boom, centred on technology investment including artificial intelligence, could drive economic growth and productivity gains over the next decade and support solid asset returns.
It projected stronger growth in advanced economies and improvements in bond returns and diversification opportunities.It also compared the investment appeal of bitcoin and gold.

extraction.body: JPMorgan has pointed to bitcoin as the asset most likely to deliver the highest return among major asset classes over the next 10 to 15 years.On Oct. 20, blockchain media outlet U.Today reported that JPMorgan, in its "2027 Long-Term Capital Markets Assumptions" report, assessed bitcoin's future annualised compound return at 10.0 percent. That is above the projections for other major asset classes in the report.U.S. real estate investment trusts were put at 8.2 percent, small-cap stocks at 7.7 percent, large-cap stocks at 7.5 percent, emerging market equities at 7.1 percent and gold at 5.5 percent. It is the first time JPMorgan has presented a return range for bitcoin in its Long-Term Capital Markets Assumptions report.The outlook also coincides with a shift in how JPMorgan views bitcoin. Matt Hougan (맷 호건), chief investment officer at Bitwise, said JPMorgan has moved from a sceptical stance on bitcoin to a stage where it is releasing long-term performance projections.JPMorgan cited expanding capital expenditure worldwide as the backdrop for the outlook. It said a $15 trillion global capital expenditure boom, centred on technology investment including artificial intelligence, could drive economic growth and productivity gains over the next decade and support solid asset returns. It projected stronger growth in advanced economies and improvements in bond returns and diversification opportunities.It also compared the investment appeal of bitcoin and gold. JPMorgan said investors still view gold more optimistically than bitcoin. Since early 2026, funds equivalent to earlier outflows have fully returned to spot gold exchange-traded funds, while spot bitcoin ETFs have recovered only about half of their outflows, it said.JPMorgan said the dynamic could instead increase bitcoin's room to rise further. Because bitcoin is less hedged than gold, its upside potential could be greater, it said. While gold is leading the recovery in inflows, bitcoin still has additional upside potential in terms of investor positioning, it said.JPMorgan previously presented $266,000 in February as bitcoin's theoretical long-term value. It calculated the figure based on a comparison with gold while reflecting bitcoin's volatility. Combined with the latest long-term expected return outlook, it amounts to JPMorgan signalling to the market that it sees bitcoin not as a short-term volatile asset but as one of the targets for long-term asset allocation.The point to watch is whether actual fund flows will follow the outlook. Attention is also focused on the pace of recovery in spot bitcoin ETF flows, relative flows against gold ETFs and how expanding technology investment will affect the broader long-term asset market.First they ignore you, then they laugh at you, then they fight at you, then they add you to their Long-Term Capital Markets Assumptions paper and predict you'll be the best-performing asset of the next decade.

extraction.body: J.P. Morgan Asset Management has included Bitcoin in its long-term return forecasts for the first time, projecting that it will deliver a higher compound annual return than gold and U.S. large-cap stocks over the next 10–15 years. According to Wu Blockchain, JPMorgan Chase’s investment arm set its expected compound annual return for Bitcoin at 10% under its 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions . This puts Bitcoin ahead of traditional investment assets in the forecasts it released. In the same set of forecasts, the expected compound annual return was 7.5% for U.S. large-cap stocks, 5.5% for gold, and 8.2% for U.S. real estate investment trusts. The projected rate for Bitcoin is 4.5 percentage points higher than gold’s and 2.5 percentage points higher than that of U.S. large-cap stocks. The comparison reflects expectations for a 10–15-year investment period rather than a price target for a single year. The firm estimated Bitcoin’s annualized volatility at 55% . This indicates that strong price swings may accompany its long-term return expectations. The arithmetic annual return expectation in the forecast set is 20.9%. The arithmetic average represents the average of periodic returns, while compound return reflects the investment’s cumulative growth rate over time; the two rates therefore represent different calculation methods. Bitwise Chief Investment Officer Matt Hougan interpreted these figures as a picture that places Bitcoin as the asset with the highest expected return over the next decade. JPMorgan’s inclusion of Bitcoin in these long-term forecasts for the first time also makes it possible to compare it directly with traditional assets, in addition to its price outlook. Everything that happened in the past 12 months—from the shallowness of the four-year pullback, to the continued progress on regulation, to the dramatic growth in demand for hard assets like gold—points to the continued long-term success of bitcoin .
That's why we're boosting our 10-year target from $1.3 million to $1.6 million," said Matt Hougan, Chief Investment Officer at Bitwise.

extraction.body: J.P. Morgan Asset Management has included Bitcoin in its long-term return forecasts for the first time, projecting that it will deliver a higher compound annual return than gold and U.S. large-cap stocks over the next 10–15 years. According to Wu Blockchain, JPMorgan Chase’s investment arm set its expected compound annual return for Bitcoin at 10% under its 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions . This puts Bitcoin ahead of traditional investment assets in the forecasts it released. In the same set of forecasts, the expected compound annual return was 7.5% for U.S. large-cap stocks, 5.5% for gold, and 8.2% for U.S. real estate investment trusts. The projected rate for Bitcoin is 4.5 percentage points higher than gold’s and 2.5 percentage points higher than that of U.S. large-cap stocks. The comparison reflects expectations for a 10–15-year investment period rather than a price target for a single year. The firm estimated Bitcoin’s annualized volatility at 55% . This indicates that strong price swings may accompany its long-term return expectations. The arithmetic annual return expectation in the forecast set is 20.9%. The arithmetic average represents the average of periodic returns, while compound return reflects the investment’s cumulative growth rate over time; the two rates therefore represent different calculation methods. Bitwise Chief Investment Officer Matt Hougan interpreted these figures as a picture that places Bitcoin as the asset with the highest expected return over the next decade. JPMorgan’s inclusion of Bitcoin in these long-term forecasts for the first time also makes it possible to compare it directly with traditional assets, in addition to its price outlook. extraction.body: Personally identifiable information belonging to thousands of U.S. Department of Homeland Security employees has been published online after a hacker stole reams of data in a previously undisclosed breach at the government department earlier this year. The breach includes names, job titles, and work contact information, such as email addresses, cell phone numbers, and office locations, of more than 40,000 people who work for the federal department, including border and immigration agents, cybersecurity staffers, and senior department officials. A hacker who goes by the handle Department of Peace claimed they obtained the data from an Okta single sign-on system used by Homeland Security to allow employees and contractors across its various agencies to log in to its central network. The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access. More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry. The data also contains records associated with another 10,000 employees of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit, and just under a 1,000 employees who work at U.S. cybersecurity defense agency CISA. Thousands of additional records relate to staff who work at the department’s headquarters and its other agencies, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen. The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out. This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit . It’s also the second breach involving Homeland Security this year, after the same hacker claimed to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and the private sector, including defense contractors and surveillance vendors. The latest batch of breached data, which appears authentic, offers a rare — albeit incomplete — view into the scale and operations of Homeland Security, whose deportations, arbitrary detentions, and killings of U.S. citizens under its leadership have become a key issue for voters ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections. The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest. TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database. The thousands of employee directory records appear to have been exfiltrated around mid-August, according to the timestamps on each person’s record. The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff . It’s unclear whether the vulnerability that allowed the breach has been fixed or if Homeland Security is aware of the data theft. A spokesperson for Homeland Security did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment about the breach. When reached, Okta said it was aware of this report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” a spokesperson said. While the leaked data includes identifiable information about agents and officers, the dataset also reveals more about the surveillance technologies and cybersecurity tools that Homeland Security employees may be able to access. Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE. The leaked data contains information about employees’ membership in user groups within the department’s Active Directory, a system that controls access to the department’s internal tools, services, and third-party offerings used for work. Most of the Homeland Security employees in the dataset were members of the user group that had access to Microsoft 365, the tech giant’s cloud service that hosts the agency’s emails and files, as well as user groups for accessing Adobe Acrobat, Citrix, and other typical desktop software. The data also shows that around 4,500 users, including ICE agents and deportation officers, are members of a group called “Headspace_users.” Online therapy provider Headspace previously had an $82,500 federal contract with ICE that ended in 2023 to fund “mental health software required for ERO employees,” a reference to ICE’s deportation unit. A spokesperson for Headspace said the company has not provided any services to DHS or ICE since 2023. Dozens of other user groups reference Penlink , a web surveillance company that makes technology it claims can track the location data of hundreds of millions of mobile devices. Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years. The user groups vary in size, from a handful of users in local Homeland Security offices around the country to more than 2,000 users across ICE’s HSI unit nationally. One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media. A spokesperson for Penlink did not respond to a request for comment. One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status . The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon. Researchers and public information advocates say that the exposed data could provide valuable leads for investigations into alleged abuses by the Trump administration, such as identifying email addresses of agents that can be used in public records requests under the Freedom of Information Act. “Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results,” said Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of transparency nonprofit Property of the People. “Given the Trump administration’s contempt for even basic transparency, the need for such tools is urgent,” said Shapiro. DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best said that the exposed Homeland Security data will be a “catalyst for investigations, empowering journalists, Congressional inquiries, legal challenges, community action and Freedom of Information Act requests.” Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch. He also authors the weekly cybersecurity newsletter, this week in security . He can be reached via encrypted message at zackwhittaker.1337 on Signal. You can also contact him by email, or to verify outreach, at [email protected] .

sources.title: Hacker stole sensitive FEMA and border patrol data in months-long breach
passages: An unidentified hacker stole sensitive data from Customs and Border Protection and Federal Emergency Management Agency employees in a “widespread” breach this summer that lasted several weeks, according to an internal FEMA assessment reviewed by CNN.

In her August 29 statement, Noem said that “no sensitive data was extracted from any DHS networks,” but the document says that on September 10, a “DHS Task Force” and FEMAs officials confirmed that the attacker stole FEMA and CBP employee data.

Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem announced the firing last month of two-dozen FEMA IT employees, including the agency’s top tech executives, blasting them for “severe lapses in security” that allowed a “threat actor to breach FEMA’s network and threaten the entire Department and the nation as a whole.” Noem appears to have been referring to the same incident described in the document obtained by CNN.
In mid-July, as the intruder navigated FEMA’s systems and attempted to extract sensitive information, DHS launched its initial efforts to contain and halt the breach.
Yet, according to the assessment, nearly two months later — by September 5 — DHS and FEMA were still trying to remediate the incident.

The incident led to an urgent cleanup operation by senior Department of Homeland Security IT officials after the hacker gained deeper access to a FEMA computer network that handles operations in a region that stretches from New Mexico to Texas to Louisiana, the document says.
It was not immediately clear if the FEMA breach is related to that activity.

Though Noem called the fired FEMA workers incompetent, some longtime FEMA officials previously told CNN that the ousted leaders were “extremely competent” and “highly respected.” The firings came on the heels of another controversy: Several agency employees had just been placed on administrative leave and later put under investigation for signing an open letter to Congress warning that the Trump administration’s overhaul of the agency was undermining disaster response and putting communities at risk.

Noem has insisted her department is “cleaning house at FEMA.” Her sweeping actions have left many high-ranking current and former officials questioning whether she is using these incidents as a pretext for a broader purge.

US cyber officials issued an “emergency directive” last week ordering federal agencies to defend their networks against an “advanced” group of hackers that have breached at least one agency in an apparent espionage campaign.
That type of software is a prime target for hackers because it can be a gateway to more sensitive parts of a network.

The document, which was presented to FEMA staff this week in an update on the breach, reveals just how easily the attacker bypassed the agency’s digital defenses.
In mid-July, as the intruder navigated FEMA’s systems and attempted to extract sensitive information, DHS launched its initial efforts to contain and halt the breach.
Yet, according to the assessment, nearly two months later — by September 5 — DHS and FEMA were still trying to remediate the incident.
“On August 29, at the time the statement was issued, there was no evidence that sensitive DHS operational data had been compromised,” a DHS spokesperson said, referring to Noem’s previous statement.

“This remains an active investigation, and we will not comment on or validate leaked internal materials.” The attacker hit software made by Citrix, a government contractor, that allows users to access networks remotely.
That type of software is a prime target for hackers because it can be a gateway to more sensitive parts of a network.
NextGov/FCW, a tech news publication, first reported on the document.

Though Noem called the fired FEMA workers incompetent, some longtime FEMA officials previously told CNN that the ousted leaders were “extremely competent” and “highly respected.” The firings came on the heels of another controversy: Several agency employees had just been placed on administrative leave and later put under investigation for signing an open letter to Congress warning that the Trump administration’s overhaul of the agency was undermining disaster response and putting communities at risk.

Noem has insisted her department is “cleaning house at FEMA.” Her sweeping actions have left many high-ranking current and former officials questioning whether she is using these incidents as a pretext for a broader purge.
At any given time, US officials are dealing with numerous hacking threats facing the sprawling confederation of federal computer systems.

US cyber officials issued an “emergency directive” last week ordering federal agencies to defend their networks against an “advanced” group of hackers that have breached at least one agency in an apparent espionage campaign.
It was not immediately clear if the FEMA breach is related to that activity.

extraction.body: Personally identifiable information belonging to thousands of U.S. Department of Homeland Security employees has been published online after a hacker stole reams of data in a previously undisclosed breach at the government department earlier this year. The breach includes names, job titles, and work contact information, such as email addresses, cell phone numbers, and office locations, of more than 40,000 people who work for the federal department, including border and immigration agents, cybersecurity staffers, and senior department officials. A hacker who goes by the handle Department of Peace claimed they obtained the data from an Okta single sign-on system used by Homeland Security to allow employees and contractors across its various agencies to log in to its central network. The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access. More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry. The data also contains records associated with another 10,000 employees of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit, and just under a 1,000 employees who work at U.S. cybersecurity defense agency CISA. Thousands of additional records relate to staff who work at the department’s headquarters and its other agencies, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen. The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out. This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit . It’s also the second breach involving Homeland Security this year, after the same hacker claimed to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and the private sector, including defense contractors and surveillance vendors. The latest batch of breached data, which appears authentic, offers a rare — albeit incomplete — view into the scale and operations of Homeland Security, whose deportations, arbitrary detentions, and killings of U.S. citizens under its leadership have become a key issue for voters ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections. The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest. TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database. The thousands of employee directory records appear to have been exfiltrated around mid-August, according to the timestamps on each person’s record. The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff . It’s unclear whether the vulnerability that allowed the breach has been fixed or if Homeland Security is aware of the data theft. A spokesperson for Homeland Security did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment about the breach. When reached, Okta said it was aware of this report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” a spokesperson said. While the leaked data includes identifiable information about agents and officers, the dataset also reveals more about the surveillance technologies and cybersecurity tools that Homeland Security employees may be able to access. Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE. sources.title: Hacker stole sensitive FEMA and border patrol data in months-long breach
passages: An unidentified hacker stole sensitive data from Customs and Border Protection and Federal Emergency Management Agency employees in a “widespread” breach this summer that lasted several weeks, according to an internal FEMA assessment reviewed by CNN.

In her August 29 statement, Noem said that “no sensitive data was extracted from any DHS networks,” but the document says that on September 10, a “DHS Task Force” and FEMAs officials confirmed that the attacker stole FEMA and CBP employee data.

Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem announced the firing last month of two-dozen FEMA IT employees, including the agency’s top tech executives, blasting them for “severe lapses in security” that allowed a “threat actor to breach FEMA’s network and threaten the entire Department and the nation as a whole.” Noem appears to have been referring to the same incident described in the document obtained by CNN.
In mid-July, as the intruder navigated FEMA’s systems and attempted to extract sensitive information, DHS launched its initial efforts to contain and halt the breach.
Yet, according to the assessment, nearly two months later — by September 5 — DHS and FEMA were still trying to remediate the incident.

The incident led to an urgent cleanup operation by senior Department of Homeland Security IT officials after the hacker gained deeper access to a FEMA computer network that handles operations in a region that stretches from New Mexico to Texas to Louisiana, the document says.
It was not immediately clear if the FEMA breach is related to that activity.

Though Noem called the fired FEMA workers incompetent, some longtime FEMA officials previously told CNN that the ousted leaders were “extremely competent” and “highly respected.” The firings came on the heels of another controversy: Several agency employees had just been placed on administrative leave and later put under investigation for signing an open letter to Congress warning that the Trump administration’s overhaul of the agency was undermining disaster response and putting communities at risk.

Noem has insisted her department is “cleaning house at FEMA.” Her sweeping actions have left many high-ranking current and former officials questioning whether she is using these incidents as a pretext for a broader purge.

US cyber officials issued an “emergency directive” last week ordering federal agencies to defend their networks against an “advanced” group of hackers that have breached at least one agency in an apparent espionage campaign.
That type of software is a prime target for hackers because it can be a gateway to more sensitive parts of a network.

sources.title: Google tells platforms to noindex link-shared pages by default - PPC Land
passages: Google today revised its Search Central guide on preventing user-generated spam , widening it beyond comment forms and hosting services to "tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps." The page gains a new section, "Only index content meant for Search," which says pages created for direct sharing, collaboration or utility should carry a noindex rule or be blocked from crawling by default, and it adds Search Console alerts and platform-level metrics to its monitoring checklist.
The change is logged in an entry posted today on Google's documentation changelog , and the page carries a "Last updated 2026-10-26 UTC" stamp.
Marketing teams use many of the kinds of services the guide now describes.
Campaign microsites, prototype landing pages, hosted forms, interactive calculators, AI-generated reports and shared chat outputs are often built on third-party platforms and passed around by link.
Google's guidance does not describe what that opt-in should look like.

When DuckDuckGo launched share links for its Duck.ai assistant on October 7, 2026, it said that shared conversations from ChatGPT and Claude had appeared in search results over the previous year, sometimes with names and personal details attached.

Security firm Claroc has cited 2025 cases in which more than 370,000 Grok conversations were indexed, figures it gave when Meta paused sharing in its Muse AI agent on October 20 after more than 6,800 share hostnames surfaced in passive DNS records.
Claroc said that exposure did not involve search engines, and that Muse's robots.txt asked crawlers to stay off its share paths.
It is filed as an update to a guide, not as a change to Google's spam policies, which live in a separate document.
That distinction carries particular weight for link-shared content.

A share link exists to be pasted elsewhere - into social posts, forums, messaging apps and emails - which is precisely the kind of external linking that can lead Google to index a blocked URL without its content.
The new section does not discuss the interaction.
Google's own products fall within the categories as well.
Neither product's coverage establishes whether its shared pages are indexed by search engines.
Google has not said whether enforcement will follow, and the guide describes no consequence for a platform that leaves shared pages indexable.

What the page does say is that spammers "may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies." Those pages can end up in Google Search even when they were only meant for the few people holding the link, which lets spammers fill results with junk hosted on someone else's trusted website. Google now says pages like that should be hidden from search by default, and that the companies running these tools should watch Search Console and their own numbers for sudden jumps in new public pages. The page is titled "Prevent user-generated spam on your site and platform." It sits in the "Preventing and monitoring abuse" part of Search Central's monitoring and debugging documentation, alongside guides on malware, phishing and deceptive sites, and the Google Safe Browsing Repeat Offenders Policy. Three passages are new or rewritten. Every other paragraph, from the reputation system for new accounts to an example about overnight traffic from Italian IP addresses on a site aimed at Japan, is unchanged word for word. The introduction previously warned that spammers exploit open comment forms, and that "hosting platforms may be similarly open to abuse," with spammers creating large numbers of sites that break Google's spam policies. The first asks services whose users create "shareable pages, generated outputs, or interactive tools" to consider whether that content is meant to be found through search engines or "only accessed directly by people with a link." "When pages are created for direct sharing, collaboration, or utility rather than public search discovery, apply the noindex rule (using a robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header) or block crawling in robots.txt by default." Everything turns on the final two words. The guide does not tell platforms to keep shared content out of Search permanently, nor does it describe what should happen when a user wants a shared page to be found. Exclusion is the starting position. How, or whether, a page later moves into the index is left unaddressed. The "Monitor your service for abuse" list gained two items, both placed at the top. The first asks operators to verify their site or subdomain in Search Console so that Google can email them if it issues a manual action against the site or detects security issues. It also names two Search Console reports, Page Indexing and Search performance, to be checked regularly for "unexpected spikes in indexed pages, impressions, or queries" that do not match what the platform is for. A share link exists to be pasted elsewhere - into social posts, forums, messaging apps and emails - which is precisely the kind of external linking that can lead Google to index a blocked URL without its content. The concern is the use of a platform's domain to publish spam rather than ranking damage to the host: in January, Mueller said that spam links in blog comments have no effect on a host site's rankings . Over the past month I've watched websites with heavy concentrations of AI-generated content, the kind Ahrefs now flags as "Very high" on its AI Content Level metric, begin sliding in Google organic search.
This also lines up with the rollout of Google’s latest June 2026 spam update that recently finished rolling out.
But when declines cluster around a specific site profile right as Google publishes both an algorithm update and research on detecting that exact profile, it deserves attention.
Google's 2023 guidance rewards content for quality regardless of production method; enforcement targets scaled content abuse, meaning high-volume, low-value pages built mainly to manipulate rankings.
A content classifier scans for repetitive, templated narratives and for high-frequency publishing behavior that no human schedule produces.
An infrastructure component ties accounts back to a common source.
When enough accounts in a cluster show the same AI-generated templates, Google removes the whole cluster at once rather than penalizing individual pages.
Automation has been part of publishing for decades, from sports scores to weather forecasts.
The risk calculus for AI-heavy SEO & AEO has changed shape.
The question used to be whether a single page looked low quality.
The question now includes whether your templates, publishing cadence, infrastructure and content similarities make your operation resemble a coordinated spam network.
Gabe's read: Google will not let companies spam their way into AI search , and marketers should expect stronger automated systems plus manual actions.
Traditional quality filters evaluate one piece of content at a time.
Google's researchers acknowledge that generative AI broke that model.
Spammers can now produce endless variations of what the paper calls functionally identical content: every page technically unique, every page effectively the same.

Its appearance in a Google paper about catching synthetic spam suggests it may have been put to that use only recently.
One more detail worth knowing: speed of adaptation.
The paper describes using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and Automatic Prompt Optimization (APO) to retune classifiers when spammers move to new generative models.
That means days of adjustment instead of months of retraining.
When the next model ships and spam operations migrate, Google can follow almost immediately.
The paper, covered by Roger Montti at Search Engine Journal and shared widely by Glenn Gabe on X , describes the Scalable Cluster Termination System.

coreStoryFacts.text: Google today revised its Search Central guide on preventing user-generated spam , widening it beyond comment forms and hosting services to "tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps." The page gains a new section, "Only index content meant for Search," which says pages created for direct sharing, collaboration or utility should carry a noindex rule or be blocked from crawling by default, and it adds Search Console alerts and platform-level metrics to its monitoring checklist.
The change is logged in an entry posted today on Google's documentation changelog , and the page carries a "Last updated 2026-10-26 UTC" stamp.
Marketing teams use many of the kinds of services the guide now describes.
Campaign microsites, prototype landing pages, hosted forms, interactive calculators, AI-generated reports and shared chat outputs are often built on third-party platforms and passed around by link.
Google's guidance does not describe what that opt-in should look like.

When DuckDuckGo launched share links for its Duck.ai assistant on October 7, 2026, it said that shared conversations from ChatGPT and Claude had appeared in search results over the previous year, sometimes with names and personal details attached.

Security firm Claroc has cited 2025 cases in which more than 370,000 Grok conversations were indexed, figures it gave when Meta paused sharing in its Muse AI agent on October 20 after more than 6,800 share hostnames surfaced in passive DNS records.
Claroc said that exposure did not involve search engines, and that Muse's robots.txt asked crawlers to stay off its share paths.
It is filed as an update to a guide, not as a change to Google's spam policies, which live in a separate document.
That distinction carries particular weight for link-shared content.

A share link exists to be pasted elsewhere - into social posts, forums, messaging apps and emails - which is precisely the kind of external linking that can lead Google to index a blocked URL without its content.
The new section does not discuss the interaction.
Google's own products fall within the categories as well.
Neither product's coverage establishes whether its shared pages are indexed by search engines.
Google has not said whether enforcement will follow, and the guide describes no consequence for a platform that leaves shared pages indexable.

What the page does say is that spammers "may create a large number of pages or sites that violate our spam policies." Those policies include scaled content abuse , which covers mass-produced pages that add little value for users, and Google stated in May 2026 that its spam policies apply to AI Overviews and AI Mode as well as to traditional results.
Those pages can end up in Google Search even when they were only meant for the few people holding the link, which lets spammers fill results with junk hosted on someone else's trusted website.
Google names no products, companies or technologies.
The words "artificial intelligence" appear nowhere on the page.
A robots.txt disallow rule works at a different stage.
It stops a crawler from fetching a URL but does not, on its own, keep that URL out of the index.
The two methods therefore do not stack, and combining them can defeat the noindex rule.
Google does not say which services prompted the change.
PPC Land's coverage over the past year has documented several types of product that match the guide's new language.

Marketing teams use many of the kinds of services the guide now describes.
Campaign microsites, prototype landing pages, hosted forms, interactive calculators, AI-generated reports and shared chat outputs are often built on third-party platforms and passed around by link.
Google's guidance does not describe what that opt-in should look like.

When DuckDuckGo launched share links for its Duck.ai assistant on October 7, 2026, it said that shared conversations from ChatGPT and Claude had appeared in search results over the previous year, sometimes with names and personal details attached.

Security firm Claroc has cited 2025 cases in which more than 370,000 Grok conversations were indexed, figures it gave when Meta paused sharing in its Muse AI agent on October 20 after more than 6,800 share hostnames surfaced in passive DNS records.

It is filed as an update to a guide, not as a change to Google's spam policies, which live in a separate document.
That distinction carries particular weight for link-shared content.

Neither product's coverage establishes whether its shared pages are indexed by search engines.

passages: The timing matters because the traffic data is already moving.

Over the past month I've watched websites with heavy concentrations of AI-generated content, the kind Ahrefs now flags as "Very high" on its AI Content Level metric, begin sliding in Google organic search.
This also lines up with the rollout of Google’s latest June 2026 spam update that recently finished rolling out.
But when declines cluster around a specific site profile right as Google publishes both an algorithm update and research on detecting that exact profile, it deserves attention.
Google's 2023 guidance rewards content for quality regardless of production method; enforcement targets scaled content abuse, meaning high-volume, low-value pages built mainly to manipulate rankings.
A content classifier scans for repetitive, templated narratives and for high-frequency publishing behavior that no human schedule produces.
An infrastructure component ties accounts back to a common source.
When enough accounts in a cluster show the same AI-generated templates, Google removes the whole cluster at once rather than penalizing individual pages.
Automation has been part of publishing for decades, from sports scores to weather forecasts.
The risk calculus for AI-heavy SEO & AEO has changed shape.
The question used to be whether a single page looked low quality.
The question now includes whether your templates, publishing cadence, infrastructure and content similarities make your operation resemble a coordinated spam network.
Gabe's read: Google will not let companies spam their way into AI search , and marketers should expect stronger automated systems plus manual actions.
Traditional quality filters evaluate one piece of content at a time.
Google's researchers acknowledge that generative AI broke that model.

Google has recently created an additional “Only index content meant for Search” section within the spam guide it updated on Oct. 26. The new section advises websites with pages made for direct sharing, collaboration or utility to set a noindex tag or use a robots.txt directive to block crawlers by default for those pages. According to Google’s changelog this is an addition relating to “blocking indexing of link-shared content.” The new section includes a link to the introductory page about robots.txt , and according to that introductory page the robots.txt file “is not a mechanism for keeping a web page out of Google.” Google’s new “Only index content meant for Search” section follows the guide’s advice on spotting spammy accounts and reads: “If your service lets users create shareable pages, generated outputs, or interactive tools, consider whether that content is meant to be found through search engines or only accessed directly by people with a link.” “When pages are created for direct sharing, collaboration, or utility rather than public search discovery, apply the noindex rule (using a robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header) or block crawling in robots.txt by default.” The guide’s opening paragraph said hosting platforms “may be similarly open to abuse.” The updated sentence adds “tools that let users publish shared pages, generated content, or web apps,” and says spammers may create a large number of “pages or sites” where it used to say sites. The previous version, last updated Dec. 10, 2025, already suggested noindex on posts from new users until they build a reputation on the platform. That advice is unchanged. Google’s robots.txt introduction says a page “that’s disallowed in robots.txt can still be indexed if linked to from other sites.” Google won’t crawl the blocked content in that case, but the URL and possibly the anchor text of links pointing to it can appear in results, without a description. Google’s page on noindex says the rule only works when robots.txt isn’t blocking the page, because otherwise “the crawler will never see the noindex rule.” Google’s “Control what you share” page , updated Oct. 21, lists robots.txt as applicable to “images and video” and noindex as applicable to “all content types.” On July 27, I confirmed that Claude’s share path was blocked by a “Disallow” directive in robots.txt. In addition, the share pages also returned a “none” value for the X-Robots-Tag HTTP response header. Google treats “none” as equal to both noindex and nofollow according to its documentation of robots meta tags . I have been unable to determine what Google saw when it initially found those links. The new spam guide from Google states you should be verifying your website or subdomain through Search Console for your platform to receive emails when it gets a manual action or has a security issue. It further suggests you check the Page Indexing report and Search performance report on an ongoing basis for “unexpected spikes” of indexed pages, impressions or queries which do not align with your platform’s intent. A new bullet under the guide’s monitoring advice suggests tracking creation and indexing at the platform level, with alerts for spikes in newly published public pages or “a small number of users generating a large share of indexable URLs.” Google’s changelog says its Oct. 26 update to the spam guide aims to help platforms “keep user-created pages that aren’t meant for Search out of the index and detect spam earlier.” For share links, generated outputs, and app pages, check that any noindex can reach Googlebot. A robots.txt rule that blocks Googlebot from those pages means Google never reads it. The Page Indexing report that Google’s new monitoring advice points to has a status called “Indexed, though blocked by robots.txt.” Google’s help for that status says to remove the block and use noindex. Share URLs that Google indexes despite a robots.txt block can appear under that status in Search Console. Follow on YouTube. Matt G. extraction.body: Google is making it easier for businesses to connect their apps to its AI experiences across Search and Gemini with the debut of its Connected Apps Platform. Introduced in Gemini and Google Search earlier this year, connected apps let users securely link and interact with popular third-party services, then use them to take specific actions. For instance, you could connect to Canva to design a flyer, or to YouTube Music to build a playlist. We’ve seen varying takes on the idea by other consumer-facing AI services like ChatGPT and Meta’s Muse. The premise is that such integrations could ultimately shift consumer behavior away from launching and using individual apps to instead using their favorite services through their preferred AI provider. However, to successfully capture and retain consumers’ attention, there have to actually be a wide range of connected apps to explore. Google’s idea is to open its doors to any business or developer that wants to reach users through Search or Gemini by allowing them to submit their own connected apps and monitor their performance. The platform preview is currently available in beta to developers in the U.S., and will allow developers to build and submit apps that can be used across Google’s products. To get started, developers would integrate with a cloud-hosted MCP (Model Context Protocol) server or Android MCP using the AppFunctions APIs, then use the Google Connected Console to register, test, and submit their app, Google explains. Essentially, this process lets devs connect their app to Google’s services so it can be used with the search giant’s AI features. Developers can also choose whether they want their app to be available via Search, the Gemini app, or both. After the app is live, developers can track traffic, latency, and error rates, and maintain control over their brand identity, such as their verified logos and authenticated accounts. Similar to how SEO allowed companies and websites to show search engine rankings, this could well be one of the initial steps for businesses that want their services to be more visible to users on the agentic web. Google already has over 50 Connected Apps available in Gemini, including from partners like Adobe, Experian, Localiza, Peloton, and others, in addition to its own expansive set of services, from Workplace and Photos to YouTube Music and Google Home. These apps will now come to Google Search over the next few weeks. Search today has fewer integrations, featuring apps like Instacart, Canva, YouTube Music, Yahoo Fantasy Football, and others. Google said meditation app Calm is another new partner on this effort, and that its app will soon launch on both Gemini and Search. The new Connected Apps platform is in public preview for U.S. developers who sign up for the waitlist. Google did not share when it would become more broadly available. sources.title: Google opens preview for third-party apps inside Search and Gemini - PPC Land
passages: The "more than 50" figure is harder to place.
PPC Land reported on August 12 that Google's own availability help article already listed 41 connected apps before that day's batch of 13 named partners, five of which were already on the list.
On October 13, Google said the Gemini app connects to "more than 40 apps" .
Today's post counts Search and Gemini together.
It does not say whether an app available in both products is counted once or twice, and the arithmetic from Google's earlier lists points to a total for Gemini alone that is already above 50.
Google is letting more companies build their apps into Google Search and the Gemini assistant, so people can do things like book a table or plan a workout without leaving Google.
For now it is a preview that opens in stages, and Google has not said what it costs, how it picks between competing apps, or what user data changes hands.
Access is opening in phases, and the post gives no fees, no list of markets and no account of how Google decides which app handles a request.
The second half of the post concerns the apps users can reach.

"To help users get more done, today we're launching the preview of our Connected Apps Platform, a unified way for more app developers to bring their capabilities directly into Gemini and Search," according to the post.
The pitch to developers is that a single build covers both.
For three of the four Gemini names, the news today is Search.
Adobe, Experian and Peloton were among the 14 connected apps Google began rolling out in Gemini on September 23 , a batch that also included Airtable, Linear, monday.com, Squarespace and Webflow.
The single build for two surfaces also fits what Google's leadership has been saying in public.
A developer registering once and switching on either product, or both, is that idea expressed as tooling.
Merchants reach shoppers through one system, and service apps such as fitness, ticketing or car rental now through another.
Connected apps change what an AI answer can do: instead of linking to a business, Search or Gemini can call the business's service directly.
When Google first brought Instacart, Canva and YouTube Music into AI Mode in Search on July 16 , AI Mode assembled a task and then sent the user to the partner to finish it.
Until now, which companies got that treatment was decided through partnerships announced in batches.
A console with a submission queue turns it into something closer to an application process, even if Google keeps the final say through review.
With no paid placement on offer, being a connected app is one of the few ways a brand can be present inside Gemini's interface at the moment a user asks for something it sells.
For brands, that routing logic plays the role ranking plays in search results.
The console's metrics - traffic, latency and error rates - tell an engineering team whether the integration works.
Neither the post nor the console view Google published shows any link to Google Ads, Google Analytics or conversion tracking.
The decision to build the platform on MCP follows more than a year of Google adopting the protocol piece by piece.
In February 2026, the Chrome team proposed WebMCP, which would let websites offer structured tools to agents instead of leaving them to screenshot analysis, page parsing and simulated clicks .
Today's platform moves MCP from a setting that individual users configure to the formal entry point for companies.
Users connecting their own servers is one thing; Google reviewing, publishing and monitoring third-party servers across its two largest AI surfaces is another.
Developers plug in via a cloud MCP server or Android AppFunctions and pick Search, Gemini or both.
What the post leaves out: fees, app ranking and data terms.

Meta's Developer Tools MCP launched on June 30, letting developers manage Meta apps through AI assistants, and on April 29 Meta opened Ads AI Connectors that let Claude and ChatGPT create and edit campaigns .
The protocol is becoming the common plumbing of agentic AI , with each platform deciding who gets to plug in and on what terms.
Google's terms, for now, are a sign-up form and a review queue.
Both routes rest on the Model Context Protocol , the open standard Anthropic introduced in November 2024 for connecting AI models to outside tools and data.
Google's platform accepts that standard rather than asking developers to adopt a proprietary format, which in principle lets a company reuse a server it already runs for other AI assistants.
The technical description fits in a single sentence.
Nothing goes live without review, though the developer, not Google, decides the publishing moment once approval is granted.

Google today opened a preview of its Connected Apps Platform, a single route for outside developers to build their services into both Google Search and the Gemini app. The announcement, posted on Google's blog by Chips Mistry, Group Product Manager for Search, and Mai Lowe, Group Product Manager for the Gemini app, introduces a Google Connected Console where developers register, test and submit apps for review, and choose which of the two products each app appears in. Google also said it has now launched more than 50 Connected Apps across Search and Gemini, naming Adobe, Calm, Experian, Localiza and Peloton among its partners. Access is opening in phases, and the post gives no fees, no list of markets and no account of how Google decides which app handles a request. Google is letting more companies build their apps into Google Search and the Gemini assistant, so people can do things like book a table or plan a workout without leaving Google. That matters to any business with an app, because these connected apps are the ones Search and Gemini can hand a task to when someone asks for help. For now it is a preview that opens in stages, and Google has not said what it costs, how it picks between competing apps, or what user data changes hands. The post is short. Dated October 28, 2026, carrying a three-minute read time and filed under Developer tools, Search and Gemini App, it runs to five paragraphs under the headline "Build and manage Connected Apps in one place." Two announcements share the space: a developer platform, and a new set of consumer integrations. On the first, the wording is direct. "To help users get more done, today we're launching the preview of our Connected Apps Platform, a unified way for more app developers to bring their capabilities directly into Gemini and Search," according to the post. Google frames the platform as a consolidation, describing it in the summary line as "a single place to build and manage apps for Search and the Gemini app." The operative word is preview. "We're opening access in phases, and will add more developers, markets, and Google products over the coming months," the post states, pointing developers to a sign-up and documentation at developers.google.com/connected-apps. The announcement does not say how many developers are admitted in the first phase, which countries or languages are covered, or when the preview ends. The reference to adding "Google products" in the plural suggests the platform is meant to reach beyond Search and Gemini at some point, though the post names no other product. The technical description fits in a single sentence. "Developers integrate with a cloud-hosted MCP server or Android MCP using the AppFunctions APIs, then use the Google Connected Console to register, test, and submit their app," according to Google. Both routes rest on the Model Context Protocol , the open standard Anthropic introduced in November 2024 for connecting AI models to outside tools and data. An MCP server publishes a list of "tools" - discrete actions such as searching inventory, checking availability or placing a booking - which an AI model can call on a user's behalf. Google's platform accepts that standard rather than asking developers to adopt a proprietary format, which in principle lets a company reuse a server it already runs for other AI assistants. That sequence places Google as a gatekeeper. Nothing goes live without review, though the developer, not Google, decides the publishing moment once approval is granted. One decision is made before review. "Before review, developers choose whether it will go live in Search, the Gemini app, or both," according to the post. The pitch to developers is that a single build covers both. The platform, Google says, "gives developers the opportunity to build once and reach high-intent users across both Search and the Gemini app." No figure accompanies "high-intent," and the post does not say how many people use Connected Apps today. After launch, the reporting is operational. "Once live, you can track traffic, latency, and error rates, and keep control of your brand identity, including verified logos and authenticated accounts," the post states. Traffic, latency and error rates are the measures an engineering team watches to keep a service running. The post mentions no conversion data, no revenue reporting and no visibility into which user requests triggered an app. The second half of the post concerns the apps users can reach. "We've launched more than 50 Connected Apps between Search and Gemini in areas ranging from productivity and event ticketing to health and fitness," according to Google. Four partners are singled out. "Integrations with partners like Adobe, Experian, Localiza, and Peloton are live for users in Gemini, and in the coming weeks, we'll be bringing these Connected Apps to Search as well," the post states. Localiza is a Brazilian car rental company; the post does not describe what its integration does or in which markets it is available. The fifth name is new across both products: "Among other apps, we'll also be launching a new integration with Calm across both Search and Gemini." For three of the four Gemini names, the news today is Search. Adobe, Experian and Peloton were among the 14 connected apps Google began rolling out in Gemini on September 23 , a batch that also included Airtable, Linear, monday.com, Squarespace and Webflow. Adobe's tools from Photoshop, Lightroom, Express and Firefly began a global rollout inside Gemini on September 24 . The "more than 50" figure is harder to place. PPC Land reported on August 12 that Google's own availability help article already listed 41 connected apps before that day's batch of 13 named partners, five of which were already on the list. Fourteen more followed in September. On October 13, Google said the Gemini app connects to "more than 40 apps" . Today's post counts Search and Gemini together. It does not say whether an app available in both products is counted once or twice, and the arithmetic from Google's earlier lists points to a total for Gemini alone that is already above 50. Google directs readers to its help center pages for Search and Gemini for the complete list. Several questions that matter to anyone weighing an integration go unanswered in the announcement. Economics. There is no mention of fees, revenue share or charges to developers, and nothing on whether users pay to reach any app beyond what the partner itself charges. Selection. When two ticketing apps or two fitness apps are both connected, which one does Search or Gemini call? The post does not describe how a request is routed, whether users must link an app before it can be used, or whether Google may suggest an app the user has not connected. For brands, that routing logic plays the role ranking plays in search results. Data. "Authenticated accounts" implies that users sign in to a partner service through Google, but the post does not describe the linking process, what user information passes from Google to the developer, what returns to Google, or how long either side keeps it. Connected apps change what an AI answer can do: instead of linking to a business, Search or Gemini can call the business's service directly. When Google first brought Instacart, Canva and YouTube Music into AI Mode in Search on July 16 , AI Mode assembled a task and then sent the user to the partner to finish it. Until now, which companies got that treatment was decided through partnerships announced in batches. A console with a submission queue turns it into something closer to an application process, even if Google keeps the final say through review. The audience on the Gemini side is large. Alphabet reported on July 22 that the Gemini app had reached 950 million monthly users . That app carries no advertising. Google's vice president of global ads, Dan Taylor, denied in December 2025 that ads were coming to Gemini , and in January said there were no plans for ads in the Gemini app . With no paid placement on offer, being a connected app is one of the few ways a brand can be present inside Gemini's interface at the moment a user asks for something it sells. The single build for two surfaces also fits what Google's leadership has been saying in public.
